media.title: Out of Every Hundred
media.context: Shown in the short why step, after students say where they have seen the % sign and before the 50% of s line.
media.description: Under a header reading "Out of Every Hundred", four panels appear side by side. The first panel shows a 10 by 10 grid of 100 squares with 25 shaded amber, captioned "25%". The second shows "₹100" pointing to 100 coins in 10 rows of 10, with 25 amber coins and 75 grey coins, labelled "25/100". The third shows a circle cut into four equal quarters with one quarter shaded amber, labelled "1/4" and captioned "25% = 25/100 = 1/4". The fourth panel displays 40 children in 4 rows of 10, highlighting the top 10, captioned "10 out of 40" and "Also 25%". Two green tags below read "per cent = per centum" and "out of every hundred".
media.teaching_notes: Point to the 100 in each panel and ask, out of every 100 of what? Then point to the fourth panel on the right: there are not 100 children, yet it is still 25%, because 10 out of 40 is 25 out of every 100. This heads off the belief that a percentage needs 100 real things.
media.negative_prompt: photorealistic rendering, photographic texture, 3D render, studio lighting or depth-of-field blur; gradients, drop shadows, bevels or glossy highlights; perspective drawn into a view that should be flat; ornamental borders, frames, mascots, emoji or speech bubbles that carry no information; watermarks, signatures, logos, stock imagery; garbled or misspelled words, invented digits, duplicated or contradictory labels, handwriting and script fonts, wording in any script other than English; text cropped at the edge, labels overlapping the object they name, type too small to read at half size; any wording at all beyond the listed labels; a grid whose rows or columns do not match the count stated; any board name, publisher name, book title, page number or curriculum branding anywhere in the frame or on any prop
media.generation_prompt:
MATHEMATICAL IMAGE REQUIREMENT
Teaching purpose: The same 25% is 25 of 100 squares, 25 of 100 rupees and one quarter of a circle, because per cent means out of every hundred.

Composition: Flat, friendly educational illustration for a middle-school maths lesson: plain white background, thin uniform dark outlines (#2B2B2B), flat fills with no shading and no gradients, clean sans-serif labels in plain classroom English a child can read aloud. Colour-blind-safe colours: teal #0072B2 for the first set, amber #E69F00 for the second set, green #009E73 for what agrees or works, reddish purple #CC79A7 for the focus, grey #6B7280 for construction; muted red #D55E00 only for a wrong or impossible case, never as decoration. 16:9 landscape, 1456 by 816 pixels. Three panels side by side above a ribbon. Left panel: a 10 by 10 grid of equal squares with 25 squares shaded amber, captioned 25%. Middle panel: a 100 rupee note on the left with an arrow to 100 one-rupee coins laid out in 10 rows of 10, 25 of them highlighted in amber. Right panel: a circle cut into four equal quarters, one quarter shaded amber, labelled 25% = 25/100 = 1/4. Bottom ribbon across the full width: per cent = per centum, then out of every hundred. A small corner inset at the bottom right shows a class of 40 children in 4 rows of 10, with 10 of them highlighted amber and the caption Also 25%.

Exact mathematical structure:
- The grid is exactly 10 by 10, 100 equal squares, with exactly 25 shaded amber.
- The shaded squares fill the first 2 rows and the first 5 squares of the third row.
- Exactly 100 one-rupee coins in 10 rows of 10, exactly 25 highlighted amber.
- The circle has exactly 4 equal quarters, exactly 1 shaded amber.
- The class inset shows exactly 40 children in 4 rows of 10, exactly 10 highlighted.
- All other squares, coins, quarters and children are left white or grey outline.

Visible text:
- 25%
- 25/100
- 1/4
- 25% = 25/100 = 1/4
- ₹100
- per cent = per centum
- out of every hundred
- 10 out of 40
- Also 25%

Critical rejection conditions:
- a grid that is not 10 by 10 or has a shaded count other than 25
- more or fewer than 25 highlighted coins, or coins not in 10 rows of 10
- circle parts of unequal size, or more than one quarter shaded
- the class inset with a count other than 40 children or other than 10 highlighted
- any count of objects, cells, ticks or dots that differs from the numbers stated above
- any text beyond the listed visible text, or any listed text misspelled or altered
- any board name, publisher name, book title, page number or curriculum branding anywhere in the frame

Student takeaway: 25% is 25 out of every 100, whatever the whole is: the same share as one quarter.

video_script.anchor: What does % mean?
video_script.design: One idea: per cent means out of every hundred, and the hundred can be a rate rather than a count. It assumes the child knows what a quarter is. The wrong idea (M7: a percent needs a hundred real things) is a common slip and is broken by cutting the test into four equal groups. Transitions: the anchor stays all video; the two signs clear before the grid; the grid shrinks to the side when the test arrives and returns beside it for the idea; one clear before the recap.
video_script.promise: you will find what the little sign says, and say it back in your own words
never_show: a stamp saying 'not a percent' left unstruck on the test of 40 marks
video_script.wrong_move: A common slip is to say a test of forty marks cannot have a percentage because it is not out of a hundred; the test is cut into four equal groups of ten, the ten scored marks fill exactly one group, and one quarter of the hundred-square grid is twenty-five squares, so the share is the same.
maths_rules: the sale board reads 25% OFF; the report card reads 25 marks out of 100
per cent comes from the Latin per centum, by the hundred; cent is a hundred; per cent = out of every 100
a Rs 100 note is worth 100 one-rupee coins; 25% of it is 25 of those coins, Rs 25
the grid is 10 x 10 = 100 equal squares; 25 squares are shaded in the part colour; 25 of 100 = 25%
25 squares are 1/4 of the grid, because 4 x 25 = 100
50% of the grid is 50 squares, half of 100; 50% of any quantity s is 50/100 x s = s/2
the test has 40 marks; 10 are scored (red); 40 = 4 x 10, so 10 of 40 = 1/4 of the test
10/40 = 25/100 (multiply top and bottom by 2.5), so 10 of 40 = 25%
in the final picture the grid and the test are drawn at the same size side by side, each stamped 25%, and the shaded share of each is exactly one quarter of its area
video_script.payoff_line: ten out of forty is the same share as twenty-five out of a hundred

final_answer.value: 25% = 25 out of every 100; 10 of 40 is also 25%
final_answer.spoken: out of every hundred

video_script.substitution: Per cent means out of every hundred, so ten out of forty is the same share as twenty-five out of a hundred.
video_script.wrong_answer: you need a hundred marks for a percent

media.title: Hundred Square
media.context: Class 8 'Fractions in Disguise', 1.1. The tool for one idea of the topic 'A Percentage Is a Fraction in Disguise': any fraction can be rebuilt as "so many out of 100". Teaching Flow v3, Pattern A (AI drives every step): the AI controls everything; nothing on screen moves unless the AI moves it. PLACEHOLDER: the tool is specified but not built yet; its url is reserved.
media.description:
The student looks at one square sheet of 100 tiles, 10 across and 10 down, with rounded corners so it reads like a sheet of postage stamps that can be torn into strips. The fraction 3/4 is written large and stacked on the left. Under the sheet a counter reads '___ out of 100' and waits to be filled. The AI runs this tool by setting the fraction, cutting the sheet and shading strips, and nothing on the screen is a button, so the student's work is to commit to a number before each move and say it aloud.

Before any cut, the student predicts how many of the 100 tiles would be red if 3/4 of the paint is red, and that guess stays on screen. The AI then draws lines that cut the sheet into 4 equal strips of 25 tiles, each tabbed with its number of parts, and asks how many tiles one strip holds and how many three strips hold. The student answers 25 and 75, three strips shade amber, the counter fills in 75 out of 100 and the tool writes = 75% in green beside the guess. Then the sheet is cleared, 2/5 is written, and the roles swap: the student tells the AI how many equal parts to cut the sheet into. The answer 5 gives 5 strips of 20 tiles, 2 strips shaded, 40 out of 100, so 40%. The sheet never changes between the two fractions, only the cutting does.

The last case is 1/3. Three strips are cut, 33 tiles shade fully, and the last tile is drawn hatched instead of shaded with a small tag 'and a bit'. The counter stops at 33 and a bit, and the AI says that 1/3 is 33.33 percent because it never lands exactly on 100, which is fine. If an answer is off, the hints come in order. First: what number do you multiply 4 by to reach 100? Then the sheet is split into 5 strips and the student says what percent one strip is, which is 20. If the student is still stuck, a worked example shows 7/20 scaled by 5 to 35/100, so 35%, and the student tries 9/25, which gives 36%. Through predicting and answering on one unchanging sheet, the student learns that a percentage is the same fraction rebuilt as so many out of 100, and that multiplying the fraction by 100 is just a shortcut for that scaling.

screen: Centre of screen: a large square made of 100 small tiles, 10 across and 10 down, with thin `grid` lines between them and slightly rounded corners on each tile so it reads as a stamp sheet rather than graph paper. Unshaded tiles are `whole`; shaded tiles are `part` (amber).
Left of the square: the fraction being worked on, written large in `ink`, a proper stacked fraction, not "3/4" inline.
Below the square: a counter reading "___ out of 100", which fills in as tiles shade. Beneath that, once the count is complete, the tool writes "= ___%" in `good`.

Cut lines: when the AI cuts the sheet into columns, thick `ink` lines animate down through the perforations over 300 ms, visibly splitting the sheet into equal strips. Each strip gets a small tab label at the top ("1 part", "2 parts"…).

The leftover case: for thirds, the final column is visibly short, 33 whole tiles and a partial tile, and the partial tile is drawn hatched, not shaded, with a small tag "and a bit". This is deliberate: students must see that some fractions do not land cleanly on 100.
Nothing is clickable. There are no buttons visible to the student. The AI drives, so the screen stays clean.
tool_config.metaphor: a sheet of postage stamps. Everybody has seen a perforated sheet of identical stamps; you can tear it into strips along the perforations. That is exactly the move this tool needs.
tool_config.one_idea: any fraction can be rebuilt as "so many out of 100".

placement.where: on its concept, after the concept video: the AI drives every step and speaks while it moves; the student watches, predicts and answers

tool_config.why_a_tool: the student needs to see the same square cut differently for 3/4, 2/5 and 1/3, the sheet never changes, only the cutting does. That is the whole insight, and it only lands when it happens repeatedly on one unchanging square.
teaching_steps: AI writes 3/4 beside the square. "Three quarters. Let us find it on this sheet of a hundred stamps."
AI draws three vertical lines, cutting the square into 4 equal columns of 25. "Four equal parts. Each column is one quarter. How many stamps in one column? Count with me, twenty-five."
AI pauses and asks: "So if one quarter is twenty-five stamps, three quarters is…?" (waits for the student)
AI shades three columns. "Seventy-five stamps, shaded. And the whole sheet is one hundred. Seventy-five out of a hundred."
Counter fills in: 75 out of 100. AI writes = 75%. "That is all percent means. Seventy-five percent."

AI clears and writes 2/5. "Your turn to tell me what to do. How many equal parts should I cut this sheet into?" (student answers 5; AI cuts into 5 columns of 20, shades 2) "Two columns, twenty each, forty stamps. Forty percent."

AI writes 1/3 and cuts into 3. "Now a tricky one. Thirty-three stamps and a bit left over. That 'bit' is why one-third is thirty-three point three three percent, it never lands exactly on a hundred. That is fine. Not every fraction is friendly."

tool_questions.note: Questions are authored when the tool is built; the teaching steps above are the brief.

tool_config.production_notes: Designed at 1280 x 720, reflowing to 360 px on a phone. Value changes animate over 300 ms ease-out. Full keyboard control, ARIA labels naming current values, 44 px minimum touch targets, WCAG AA contrast. No timers, no scores, no buzzers.

That is the whole insight, and it only lands when it happens repeatedly on one unchanging square.

content.text:
Textbook text (verbatim):
1.1 Fractions as Percentages
You might have heard statements like, “Mega Sale - up to 50% off!” or “Hiya scored 83% in her board exams”.
Do you know what the symbol ʻ%ʼ means?
This symbol is read as per cent.
The word ‘per cent’ is derived from the Latin phrase ‘per centum’, meaning ‘by the hundred’ or ‘out of hundred’.
So, 25 per cent (25%) means 25 out of every 100 - like 25 people out of 100, 25 rupees out of 100 rupees, or 25 marks out of 100 marks.
If we say 50% of some quantity s, it means
50% = 50 × 1/100 × s (50 times the unit fraction of s)
= 50/100 × s = 1/2 s.
Thus, percentages are simply fractions where the denominator is 100. Examples:
20% = 20/100 = 2/10 = 1/5,
33% = 33/100.
We saw that percentages are just fractions. Given any fraction, can we express it as a percentage? Yes, let us see how.

Teaching plan:
1. Ask where the student has seen % (sale boards, marks). Accept everything.
2. Short why: per cent means per hundred. Show image I1: the same 25% as 25 of 100 squares, 25 of 100 rupees and 25 of 100 marks. The number of real things does not have to be 100; out of every 100 is a rate (this heads off M7).
3. Read the 50% of s line: 1/100 of s is one tiny piece; 50 pieces make half.
4. The class inset of I1: 10 of 40 children highlighted is also 25%, because 10 out of 40 is 25 out of every 100.

content.text:
Textbook text (verbatim):
Expressing Fractions as Percentages
Example 1: Surya wants to use a deep orange colour to capture the sunset. He mixes some red paint and yellow paint to make this colour. The red paint makes up 3/4 of this mixture. What percentage of the colour is made with red?
3/4 is 3 out of every 4.
That is, 6 out of every 8 (equivalent fraction).
That is, 30 out of every 40.
That is, 75 out of every 100.
This means 75%.
(Side: 3/4 = 6/8 = 30/40 = 75/100)
Explaining this in a different way: To express 3/4 as a percentage, we need to find its equivalent fraction with 100 as the denominator. Two ways of going ahead are shown below.
Method 1: 3/4 = (3 × 25)/(4 × 25) = 75/100 = 75%
Method 2: 3/4 = x/100. 3/4 × 100 = x/100 × 100 [multiply both sides by 100] x = 3/4 × 100 = 75.
So, 3/4 can be expressed as 75%.
Observe the following bar model diagram showing the equivalence between 3/4 and 75%.
(Bar model: 0, 1/4, 2/4 = 1/2, 3/4, 4/4 = 1 above; 0, 25/100 (25%), 50/100 (50%), 75/100 (75%), 100/100 (100%) below)
Can you tell what percentage of the colour was made using yellow?
Example 2: Surya won some prize money in a contest. He wants to save 2/5 of the money to purchase a new canvas. Express this quantity as a percentage.
Try to understand the different methods for solving this problem, as shown below.
Method 1: 2/5 = 20/50 = 40/100 = 40%.
Method 2: 2/5 = x/100. x = 2/5 × 100 = 40.
Try completing Method 3 by filling the boxes.
Method 3 (bar: 0, 1/5, 2/5, 3/5, 4/5, 5/5 = 1 above, “Savings for canvas” shaded over 2/5, “Total prize money”; below 0% … boxes … 100%)
(Speech bubble) Isn’t it the same as finding 2/5 th of 100?
Several problems in mathematics can be approached and solved in different ways. While the method you came up with may be dear to you, it can be amusing and enriching to know how others thought about it.
A fraction is of a unit, while a percentage is per 100. Therefore, to express a fraction as a percentage, we can just multiply the fraction by 100.

content.text:
Textbook text (verbatim):
Well, if percentages are just a particular type of fraction, why do we need them? Why can’t we just continue using fractions?
Let us consider an example.
A biscuit-making factory is experimenting with 2 new varieties of biscuits. Sugar makes up 9/34 of Variety 1 and 13/45 of Variety 2. Which variety is more sugary? It may not be clear at first glance and we may have to do some calculations. But, when the same information is presented as - Sugar makes up 26.47% of Variety 1 and 28.88% of Variety 2, it is immediately clear which variety is more sugary.
If we want to have the same denominator, why choose 100 in particular? Why not 10, 50, 1000, or 43? Think.
In principle, we could choose any number as the denominator. But with 100, there are some advantages. Since our number system is base 10, numbers like 10, 100, and 1000 fit easily with decimals. For example, 31% = 31/100 = 0.31.
Converting between fractions, decimals, and percentages becomes quick and intuitive.
The number 100 is round, and easy to understand and work with. We could say “per 1000” or “per 100,000” (this usage is present in statistics like “per thousand people” or “per lakh”), but 100 hits the sweet spot - it’s large enough to give detail, yet simple enough to grasp mentally. Per 10 would be too small for many purposes.
(Side box) 9/34 = 26.47 percent (per 100); 9/34 = 2.647 per decem (per 10); 9/34 = 264.7 per mille (per 1000)
Long before the decimal fraction was introduced, the need for it was felt in computations by tenths, twentieths, and hundredths. The idea of ‘per hundred’ can be found as early as the 4th century BCE in Kautilya’s Arthaśhāstra, “An interest of a pana and a quarter per month per cent is just. Five panas per month per cent is commercial interest. Ten panas per month per cent prevails among forests. Twenty panas per month per cent prevails among sea traders”.
Around the same time, the Romans used taxes of 1/20, 1/100 in transactions related to trade and auctions. In the Italian manuscripts of the 15th century, expressions such as ‘xx p cento’, ‘x p cento’, ‘vii p cento’ can be found (equivalent to our 20%, 10%, and 7%).
Percentages Around Us
Percentages are widely used in a variety of contexts. Here are some interesting findings that involve percentages.
The human body, on average, is about 60% water by weight. - Ice cream is about 30 - 50% air by volume. - 45% of the world’s population watched at least part of the 2022 FIFA World Cup. - Over 80% of the teenagers globally fail to meet the recommendation of at least one hour of daily physical activity. - About 99.86% of the Solar System’s mass is contained in the Sun. - An estimated 52% of the agricultural land worldwide is degraded.

content.text:
How to teach:
1. Give the student 20 seconds to decide which biscuit is more sugary from 9/34 and 13/45. They will hesitate. Then show 26.47% against 28.89%, and it is instant. That hesitation is the reason percentages exist.
2. Why 100? is a one-minute talk. Mention the Arthaśāstra: Indian traders used per hundred over 2000 years ago.
3. The student picks one fact card and turns it into a sentence (for example, 60% water means a 50 kg person carries about 30 kg of water).

content.text:
How the AI teaches this:
1. Set the trap first. "Quick, which biscuit has more sugar: one where sugar is nine thirty-fourths, or one where it is thirteen forty-fifths? You have five seconds." The student cannot do it. That is the point.
2. Then release it. "Now: twenty-six point five percent, or twenty-eight point nine percent? Instant, isn't it. Same question. That hesitation you just felt, that is exactly why percentages were invented."
3. Why a hundred? "Why not out of ten? Too coarse, you could not tell 26.5 from 28.9. Why not out of a thousand? Too fussy for daily talk. A hundred sits in the sweet spot. And it fits our number system, so 31% is just 0.31."
4. A moment of pride. "This is not a new European idea, by the way. Kautilya's Arthaśāstra was setting interest rates 'per hundred' in the fourth century BCE. Traders here have been thinking in percentages for over two thousand years."
5. Make it real. Offer the fact cards, the body is 60% water, ice cream is 30 to 50% air, 99.86% of the Solar System's mass is the Sun, and ask the student to turn one into a sentence about themselves. "You weigh about forty kilos. So how much of you is water?"

video_script.anchor: 15 of Nandini's 25 marbles are white. What percent are white?
video_script.design: One idea: turn the count into out of every hundred. It assumes multiplying a fraction's top and bottom by the same number. The wrong idea (the count fifteen is the percent) is a common slip and is broken by comparing fifteen out of a hundred with a bag that is mostly white. Transitions: the bag of twenty-five stays from the hook to the idea, where it is copied four times; one clear, before the recap.
video_script.wrong_move: A common slip is to grab the fifteen from the question and say fifteen percent; fifteen out of a hundred is less than one fifth, but more than half of Nandini's marbles are white, so the picture rules it out.
maths_rules: Nandini has 25 marbles; 15 are white, 10 are not
the choices are (i) 10% (ii) 15% (iii) 25% (iv) 60% (v) 40% (vi) None of these
25 x 4 = 100, so copy the bag 4 times: 4 x 15 = 60 white marbles out of 100
the wrong 15% is 15 out of 100, less than 1/5 (20%); 15 of 25 is more than half, because half of 25 is 12.5
60% is more than half, which agrees with 15 of 25 being more than half
video_script.payoff_line: sixty percent of her marbles are white

final_answer.spoken: sixty percent

video_script.substitution: Out of every hundred marbles, how many would be white? Four bags of twenty-five make a hundred.

video_script.anchor: 15 of the 80 students walk to school. What percent walk?
video_script.design: One idea: halve until the bottom goes into a hundred, then multiply. It assumes halving decimals and scaling a fraction. The wrong idea (adding to reach a hundred) is a common slip and is broken by running the adding trick on one half. Transitions: the anchor stays all video; the working band builds the chain of fractions from the ground to the idea; one clear, before the recap.
video_script.wrong_move: A common slip is to add twenty to eighty to reach a hundred and add twenty to fifteen too, getting thirty-five percent; the same trick on one half, adding ninety-eight to both, gives ninety-nine out of a hundred, so adding changes the share.
maths_rules: 15 of 80 students walk; the fraction is 15/80
100 / 80 = 1.25, not a whole number, so 80 does not go into 100 a whole number of times
check by the other route: 15/80 x 100 = 1500/80 = 18.75
the slip: 80 + 20 = 100 and 15 + 20 = 35, giving 35/100 = 35%, which is wrong
the same adding trick on 1/2: 1 + 98 = 99 and 2 + 98 = 100, giving 99/100 = 99%, but 1/2 is 50%, so adding changes the share
estimate: 1/5 of 80 = 16 is 20%; 15 is a bit less than 16, so the answer is a bit under 20%
video_script.payoff_line: eighteen point seven five percent of the students walk

final_answer.spoken: eighteen point seven five percent

video_script.substitution: Halve the top and the bottom until the bottom goes into a hundred, then multiply both by the same number.

media.teaching_notes: One idea: when the bottom number does not go into a hundred, halve it until it does, or multiply the fraction by a hundred. Watch for the adding slip, where a child adds the same number to top and bottom to reach a hundred.

video_script.anchor: Madhu: 25% sugar. Madhav: 35% sugar. Who ate more sugar?
video_script.design: One idea: a percentage needs its whole; 'percent of what?'. Assumes: percent means out of a hundred. Wrong idea: to compare 25 and 35 directly; the one-biscuit picture breaks it before the weights arrive. Transitions: the anchor question stays all video; the two packets carry from the hook into the ground and break; the packets resize into the two bars at the start of the idea part; one clear, before the recap.
never_show: the card '35 > 25, so Madhav' left standing as a reason
26 g of sugar for the first
25.5 g of sugar for the second
video_script.wrong_move: A common slip is to compare the two percentages as if they were amounts; the picture keeps the percentages and changes only how much each child ate (Madhav one biscuit, Madhu the whole packet), and Madhu's sugar pile becomes far bigger, so the percentages alone cannot decide.
maths_rules: Madhu's biscuits: 25% sugar, so 25 g of sugar in every 100 g of biscuit; Madhav's: 35% sugar, so 35 g in every 100 g
the two packets are first drawn the same size, with no weight shown; the weight labels read '? g' until the idea part

break picture: Madhav eats one biscuit and Madhu eats the whole packet; the sugar piles are drawn in proportion to (35% of one biscuit) and (25% of a whole packet), and Madhu's pile is clearly the taller; no grams are written in this picture
Madhu ate 120 g: 120 = 100 + 20; 100 g gives 25 g; 20 g is 1/5 of 100 g, so it gives 25 / 5 = 5 g; 25 + 5 = 30 g; check 25/100 x 120 = 30
Madhav ate 95 g: 1 g of biscuit holds 35/100 = 0.35 g of sugar; 95 x 0.35 = 33.25 g; mental route 100 x 0.35 = 35, 5 x 0.35 = 1.75, 35 - 1.75 = 33.25
bars: Madhu's bar is 120 units long with 25% shaded (30 g); Madhav's bar is 95 units long with 35% shaded (33.25 g); bar lengths are in the ratio 120 : 95
33.25 > 30, so Madhav ate more sugar; the gap is 33.25 - 30 = 3.25 g, so the two sugar piles are drawn almost the same height
your turn (never shown): 130 g of biscuit with 20% sugar gives 20/100 x 130 = 26 g; 85 g with 30% sugar gives 30/100 x 85 = 25.5 g; the first has more sugar, although her percentage is smaller
video_script.payoff_line: Madhav ate more sugar, thirty-three point two five grams against thirty

final_answer.value: Madhu 30 g, Madhav 33.25 g, so Madhav
final_answer.spoken: Madhav, thirty-three point two five grams against thirty grams

narration: <bookmark mark='four'/>You need only four blocks, and each one has a shortcut.

<bookmark mark='ten'/>Ten percent moves the decimal point one place to the left.
<bookmark mark='five'/>Five percent is half of ten percent.
<bookmark mark='one'/>One percent moves the point two places to the left.
<bookmark mark='why'/>Why does ten percent move the point?

<bookmark mark='share'/>Sharing a number into ten equal parts moves each digit one place smaller.

maths_rules: the bill is 287 rupees; the sign reads 15% OFF
the four blocks: 50% = half; 10% = one tenth, the decimal point moves one place left; 5% = half of 10%; 1% = one hundredth, the point moves two places left
10% of 287 = 28.7 (28 rupees 70 paise); the point in 287.0 is drawn moving one place left
5% of 287 = 28.7 / 2 = 14.35; half of 28 is 14 and half of 0.7 is 0.35

the slip card: 287 - 15 = 272; the bill is drawn as two full hundreds and a third hundred that is 87 long; each hundred loses 15 rupees, so the cut for 300 would be 3 x 15 = 45 rupees; 287 is a little under 300, so the true cut is a little under 45
15% = 10% + 5%, so 15% of 287 = 28.7 + 14.35 = 43.05 rupees (43 rupees and 5 paise); 43.05 < 45 as predicted
recipes shown: 30% = 10% x 3; 95% = 100% - 5%; no numbers are worked for them; 95% is used, not the flow's 90%, so that the next question's 90% is not pre-solved
the blocks add because they are percentages of the same whole: 10/100 x 287 + 5/100 x 287 = 15/100 x 287
video_script.payoff_line: fifteen percent of the bill is forty-three rupees and five paise

final_answer.spoken: forty-three rupees and five paise

video_script.substitution: Ten percent is one tenth, so the decimal point moves one place left, and every other percentage is built from that block and its half, its double, or the whole.
open_questions: The Teaching Flow's version also gives the recipes 75% = 50% + 25% and 55% = 50% + 5%, which are the answers to the next question ('The Awkward Ones'). This script shows 30% (not in the table or that question) and 95% = 100% - 5% (the flow's 'knock it off the whole' idea, moved off 90% so that The Awkward Ones is not pre-solved) and leaves 75%, 90%, 70% and 55% for the child; Image I2 still shows all the recipes.

media.teaching_notes: One idea: any percentage of one whole can be built from the blocks 50%, 10%, 5% and 1%, because percentages of the same whole add. Watch for the slip of treating 15% off as 15 rupees off.

interaction_points.prompt: Next time a percentage looks awkward, which blocks will you use?

video_script.anchor: How would you find 75%, 90%, 70% and 55% of 80 grams?
video_script.design: One idea: a recipe from the blocks, and the shorter journey. Assumes: the four blocks and the 10% shortcut. Wrong idea: to take away ten grams for ten percent. Transitions: the question and the packet of 80 stay in the anchor all video; the block values from the hint stay in the working band through the idea part; one clear, before the recap.
video_script.wrong_move: A common slip is to find 90% of 80 as 80 take away 10 = 70, taking away ten grams instead of ten percent; beside it, 10% of 80 is 8, so the wrong 70 is struck.
maths_rules: the packet holds 80 grams; the blocks for 80: 50% = 40, 10% = 8, 5% = 4, 25% = half of 40 = 20, 20% = 2 x 8 = 16
the slip: 80 - 10 = 70 takes away 10 grams, not 10% of 80 (which is 8)
every answer lies between 40 (half) and 80 (the whole), because every percentage asked is between 50% and 100%
the grams are drawn as 80 dots in 8 rows of 10, so 10% is one row; half is 4 rows
video_script.payoff_line: Seventy-five percent is half, plus half of that half

final_answer.spoken: seventy-five is half plus a quarter, ninety is the whole minus ten percent, seventy is half plus twenty percent, fifty-five is half plus five percent

video_script.substitution: Every percentage is a recipe of the blocks, and 90% is the whole with 10% taken off.
open_questions: The Teaching Flow's closing line says 'above fifty, start from the whole and subtract', but its own working builds 75%, 70% and 55% up from half. This script says instead: near a hundred, start from the whole; near fifty, start from half.

media.teaching_notes: One idea: say a recipe from the blocks before computing; near 100% start from the whole and take away, near 50% start from half and build up. Watch for the slip of taking away 10 things instead of 10%.

media.title: How do you write 5% as a fraction and as a decimal?
media.context: Class 8 'Fractions in Disguise'. Question video: one question from the book. It opens only after the student has tried the question, and it hints before it tells. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: The book's percent, fraction and decimal table for 50%, 100%, 25%, 75%, 10%, 1%, 5% and 43%, pictured as shares of one bar. Each percent goes over 100, is cut down, and is read in hundredths; a common slip writes 5% as 0.5.

video_script.why: How do you write each percent as a fraction and as a decimal without mixing up tenths and hundredths?

<bookmark mark='coat'/>Three forms, one amount, so pick whichever form makes your working lighter.

video_script.anchor: Write 50%, 100%, 25%, 75%, 10%, 1%, 5% and 43% as a fraction and as a decimal.
video_script.design: One idea: percent means hundredths, so every percent has a fraction form and a decimal form. Assumes: cutting fractions down, place value to hundredths. Wrong idea: to write 5% as 0.5. Transitions: the table stays in the anchor all video and fills column by column; the bar stays on the stage through the break and the idea; one clear, before the recap.
video_script.wrong_move: A common slip is to write 5% as 0.5; the bar shows 0.5 filling half the bar, which is 50%, ten times too much, so the wrong decimal is struck.
maths_rules: percent means out of 100: x% = x/100
50% = 50/100 = 1/2 = 0.5 (given in the book's table)
5% = 5/100 = 1/20 = 0.05 (divide top and bottom by 5)
43% = 43/100 = 0.43; 43 is prime and shares no factor with 100, so the fraction does not cut down
the bar is one whole; the drawn fill for each share is that fraction of the bar: 0.5 fills half, 0.05 is a thin sliver
the wrong 0.5 for 5%: 0.5 = 50/100 = 50%, which is 10 times 5%
video_script.payoff_line: Five percent is one twentieth, nought point nought five

final_answer.spoken: one half and nought point five, one and one point nought, one quarter and nought point two five, three quarters and nought point seven five, one tenth and nought point one, one hundredth and nought point nought one, one twentieth and nought point nought five, forty-three hundredths and nought point four three

video_script.substitution: Percent means hundredths, so write it over 100, cut the fraction down, and read the decimal with two places after the point.
video_script.wrong_answer: five percent is nought point five
video_script.fraction_reading: one quarter, three quarters, one tenth, one hundredth, one twentieth, forty-three hundredths

media.title: Piece to Whole
media.context: Class 8 'Fractions in Disguise', 1.2. The tool for one idea of the topic 'Taking a Percentage of Something Real': a known part gives you one piece; pieces build the whole. Teaching Flow v3, Pattern A (AI drives every step): the AI controls everything; nothing on screen moves unless the AI moves it. PLACEHOLDER: the tool is specified but not built yet; its url is reserved.
media.description:
A long bar runs nearly the full width of the screen, and most of it lies under a grey cloth with a wavy, hand-drawn edge. Only the left stretch shows, in blue, labelled 92 km with a small tag 'this is 40%'. Below the bar is a row of empty dashed boxes waiting to be filled. The AI moves everything and nothing is clickable, so the student estimates, works out the size of one block and says what they find aloud.

First the student says whether the whole trip from Delhi to Agra is more or less than 92 km, and then holds a number for how long it really is. That guess is kept for the end. The AI cuts the bar into 5 equal blocks, and the visible 92 km turns out to lie on exactly 2 of them, because 40% is two fifths. The AI asks how much one block is when 92 is shared between 2 blocks, and the student answers 46. The dashed boxes then fill left to right as the count goes 46, 92, 138, 184, 230. The cloth lifts slowly, which is the one slow, deliberate movement of the tool, and the whole bar reads 230 km with the remaining stretch of 138 km lit up in amber. Last, the student's guess drops onto the bar as a small amber flag with the guessed number, so the gap between guess and truth is seen and not only stated.

A student who adds 40% of 92 to 92 and gets 128.8 km is taken back to the blocks: the 92 km fills only 2 of the 5 blocks, so the 40% belongs to the whole trip and not to the 92. The hints come in order. First: if 40% is 92 km, what is 20%? Then: how many 20% pieces make 100%? A retry follows on the same cloth with a book where 30% is 60 pages, so 140 pages are left. Through estimating and then building up block by block, the student learns that a known part gives the size of one piece and the pieces build the whole, which is the reverse of taking a percentage of a known whole.

screen: Centre: a long horizontal bar running nearly the full width, representing the whole journey. Most of it lies under a grey cloth (`whole` with a soft fabric texture and a slightly wavy, hand-drawn edge, it must look like cloth, not a grey rectangle).
The uncovered stretch at the left is filled `fill` (blue) and carries its value in a label above it: 92 km. A small tag beneath reads "this is 40%".
Below the bar: a row of empty piece-boxes, drawn as dashed outlines. They fill in one at a time, left to right, as the AI counts, each filled box shows its value in `part`.

The cloth lift: when the AI lifts the cloth, it animates upward and off-screen over 500 ms (slower than the standard 300 ms, this is the reveal and it should feel like one). Underneath, the full bar is shown with the total at its right end and the remaining stretch highlighted in `part`.
The guess flag: the student's earlier guess is dropped onto the bar as a small amber pennant with the guessed number on it, so the gap between guess and truth is visible, not just stated.
Nothing is clickable. The AI drives.
tool_config.metaphor: a cloth thrown over something on a table. You can see a corner of it and have to work out how big the whole thing is. Every student has done this with a wrapped gift.
tool_config.one_idea: a known part gives you one piece; pieces build the whole.

placement.where: on its concept, after the concept video: the AI drives every step and speaks while it moves; the student watches, predicts and answers

tool_config.why_a_tool: the cloth is the point. Seeing the unknown revealed block by block is what kills the "add 40% to 92" instinct, and a static picture cannot do the uncovering.
teaching_steps: AI shows the bar, cloth covering most of it, uncovered stretch labelled 92 km, and a tag "this is 40%". "Here is the whole trip, mostly hidden. We can only see ninety-two kilometres of it, and we are told that is forty percent."

AI asks first: "Before I uncover anything, is the whole trip more than ninety-two, or less?" (student answers: more) "Good. And roughly how much more? Take a guess. Two hundred? Three hundred? Hold your number."
AI cuts the bar into 5 equal blocks; the uncovered part turns out to be exactly 2 blocks. "Forty percent is two-fifths, so five blocks. And look, the visible part is exactly two of them."
AI splits the 92 label across the two blocks. "Ninety-two shared between two blocks. How much is one block?" (waits) "Forty-six."
AI fills every remaining block with 46, one at a time, counting aloud. "Forty-six… ninety-two… a hundred thirty-eight… a hundred eighty-four… two hundred thirty. The cloth comes off."
Cloth lifts. Whole bar reads 230 km; remaining stretch highlighted 138 km. "Two hundred thirty in total. One thirty-eight still to ride."
AI drops the student's guess onto the bar as a flag. "And here is where your guess landed. Look how close you were. Guessing is not cheating, it is how you build a feel for numbers."

media.title: Target Meter
media.context: Class 8 'Fractions in Disguise', 1.2. The tool for one idea of the topic 'Taking a Percentage of Something Real': 100% is a mark on a scale, not the end of it. Teaching Flow v3, Pattern A (AI drives every step): the AI controls everything; nothing on screen moves unless the AI moves it. PLACEHOLDER: the tool is specified but not built yet; its url is reserved.
media.description:
A tall, narrow glass tube fills the left two thirds of the screen, like the fundraising thermometer painted outside a school gate. A bold line labelled TARGET, 100%, Rs 5000 crosses it only about two fifths of the way up, so a long stretch of empty tube is left above the line, with faint tick marks at 150%, 200% and 250%. On the right a large figure shows the day's sales, and under it a percentage reading counts up as the liquid rises. The AI pours the amounts and nothing is clickable, so the student reads the meter and says the percentages aloud.

On Day 1 Rs 2000 is poured and the blue liquid stops well short of the line. The student says what percent of the target that is, and 40% appears. Day 2 pours Rs 3500, which is 70%, and Day 3 pours Rs 5000, where the liquid sits exactly on the line at 100%. Day 4 pours Rs 6000, and the liquid does not stop at the line. It rises into the empty tube above and turns purple, which tells the student this is new territory. The student says how much sticks out above the line, Rs 1000, and what part of 5000 that is, a fifth or 20%, so the whole reading is 100% plus 20%, which is 120%, or 6/5, or 1.2. Then Rs 7800 and Rs 9550 are poured and the student gives the percentages alone, 156% and 191%.

After that the AI runs the meter backwards. It sets 150% and then 210%, the liquid rises to those marks, and the student works out the rupees before the figure counts up to check: Rs 7500 and Rs 10,500. A wrong answer is first met with a hint: is 7800 more or less than the target, and by how much? Then: 2800 out of 5000 is what percent, and add that to 100%. A student who believes a percentage cannot pass 100 is answered by the picture itself, because the liquid has already passed the line. Through reading the meter both ways, the student learns that 100% is the whole target and not the end of the scale, so a result that beats the target is more than 100%.

screen: Left two-thirds: a tall vertical meter, drawn as a narrow tube with rounded ends, running most of the screen height. It is deliberately drawn so the target line sits at only about 40% of the tube's height, there is a lot of visible empty tube above it. That empty space is the teaching device and must never be cropped.
The target line: a bold horizontal `ink` line across the tube, roughly 40% up, with a flag label to its right reading TARGET · 100% · ₹5000.

The liquid: fills from the bottom in `fill` (blue) below the line. The moment it passes the line it changes to `beyond` (purple), the colour change is what tells the student they have crossed into new territory.
Right third: the day's figure in large `ink` (e.g. Day 4, ₹6000) and, below it, the percentage reading which counts up as the liquid rises.
Overflow marks: faint tick marks continue up the empty tube at 150%, 200%, 250% so that "above the line" is already a labelled place before the student gets there.
Reverse mode: the AI can set a percentage instead, and the liquid rises to it while the rupee figure counts up, same tube, arrow of reasoning reversed.
Nothing is clickable.

tool_config.why_a_tool: the blank space above the target line is doing the teaching. The student has to see the meter refuse to stop at 100 before they believe percentages can.
teaching_steps: AI sets the target line at ₹5000 and labels it 100%. "This line is the target. Five thousand rupees. We are calling it one hundred percent."
AI pours in ₹2000; the meter rises to below the line. "Day one, two thousand. Look where it lands. Not even half way."
AI asks: "What percent is that?" (waits) AI shows 40%.
AI pours ₹3500 to 70%, then ₹5000 to exactly the line. "Day three, he hits it exactly. The meter sits right on the line. A hundred percent."
AI pours ₹6000. The liquid rises past the line into the blank space above, which turns a different colour. "Day four, six thousand. And the meter does not stop at the line. It keeps going."
AI asks: "How much is sticking out above the line?" (waits, ₹1000) "And a thousand is what part of five thousand? A fifth, twenty percent. So the whole thing is a hundred and twenty percent."
AI pours ₹7800 and ₹9550. "Your turn to tell me the percentages." (156% and 191%)
AI runs it backwards: sets 150% and 210% and asks for the rupees. (₹7500 and ₹10,500)

tool_questions.note: Questions are authored when the tool is built; the teaching steps above are the brief.

content.text:
Textbook text (verbatim):
1.2 Percentage of Some Quantity
Example 1: Madhu and Madhav each ate biscuits of a different variety. Madhu’s biscuits had 25% sugar, while Madhav’s had 35% sugar. Can you tell who ate more sugar?
As we just saw, percentages represent fractional quantities or proportions. It would be inappropriate to compare just the percentages when they are referring to different quantities or wholes. That is, if they both had 100 g of biscuits, then clearly Madhav ate more sugar - 35 g (35% of 100 g is 35 g per 100 g) vs. Madhu’s 25 g (25% of 100 g is 25 g per 100 g).
Suppose Madhu ate 120 g of biscuits and Madhav ate 95 g of biscuits. Who consumed more sugar? Try to find out.
We know that the weight of sugar is proportional to the weight of the biscuits consumed. Madhu ate 120 g of biscuits having 25% sugar. The amount of sugar he ate is the value in the blank  - 
25 : 100 :: ____ : 120.
A few ways of going forward are shown.
(Way 1) 25% sugar means - 25 g sugar per 100 g of biscuits, which means 5 g sugar per 20 g biscuits, so 30 g sugar per 120 g biscuits.
(Way 2) The proportional relationship can be written as 25/100 = s/120. s = 25/100 × 120 = 30.
(Way 3, bar) 0, 25%, 50%, 75%, 100% ↔ 0, 30 g, 60 g, 90 g, 120 g
Do any of the methods match your thinking? Were you able to understand all the methods?
Now, let us find out how much sugar Madhav ate. He ate 95 g of biscuits with 35% sugar. Sometimes the numbers may not be convenient to calculate using different methods as we did just before.
100 g of the biscuits he ate has 35 g of sugar. (Side: 35/100 = x/1 → x = 35/100)
This means, 1 g of the biscuits has 35/100 g of sugar.
We can say that 95 g of the biscuit will have 35/100 g × 95 = 33.25 g.
This can also be solved by finding the value of s in the proportional relationship 35/100 = s/95.
Therefore, Madhav ate more sugar.
More generally, y% of some value, say 80, is given by y/100 × 80.
We can also say that 45% of some value, say z, is given by 45/100 × z.

content.text: Guided discovery. Guiding question: Madhav's biscuits are sweeter (35% against 25%). Does that guarantee he ate more sugar? Prediction: Yes, No or Depends. Most say Yes, which is what we want to test. Explore: Bar model, two bars stacked: Madhu's bar is 120 g long at 25%; Madhav's is 95 g at 35%. The student reads 30 g and 33.25 g. Then ask: what if Madhav had eaten less? Below about 85.7 g, Madhu wins. The student finds this switch-over point by trying weights. The discovery: the percentage alone cannot tell us; we need percentage and whole together.

content.text:
Teaching plan (logic first):
1. 25% sugar is a rate: 25 g in every 100 g. The actual amount depends on how much was eaten, the whole.
2. The three methods are a menu. Unitary: 25 g per 100 g, so 5 g per 20 g, so 30 g per 120 g. Proportion: 25/100 = s/120. Bar: read it off. For awkward numbers (95 g), the per 1 g unitary step always works.
3. Generalise last: y% of a value is y/100 × value.

content.text:
Textbook text (verbatim):
Free-hand Computations
We just calculated 25% of 120. Is 25% the same as 1/4 th (a quarter)?
Suppose we want to find 25% of 40. Is it the same as 1/4 th of 40?
Yes, since 25 is 1/4 th (a quarter) of 100 (25/100 = 1/4).
Therefore 25% of 40 = 25/100 × 40 is the same as 1/4 × 40.
Try to calculate (without using pen and paper) the indicated percentages of the values shown in the table below. Write your answers in the table.
(Table: columns 100, 200, 50, 80, 10, 35, 287; rows 25% (first cell 25), 10%, 20%, 5%)
How did you find these values? Discuss the methods with the class.
Do you find anything interesting in the table? (Math Talk)
You may have noticed that 20% of a value is double that of 10% of the same value. This will always happen as 20% (20 parts out of 100) is twice that of 10% (10 parts out of 100).
Using this understanding, mentally calculate how much 40% of the values in the table above would be.
What relationship do you observe among 20%, 5% and 25% of a value?
It appears that (20% of y) + (5% of y) = 25% of y. We can verify that this property always holds:
(20/100 × y) + (5/100 × y) = (25/100 × y).
Using this observation, mentally calculate how much 15% of the values in the table would be.
Suppose you have to mentally calculate the following percentages of some value: 75%, 90%, 70%, 55%. How would you do it? Discuss. (Math Talk)

Teaching plan:
1. Short why: percentages can be built from blocks, because the % of the same whole add up. Anchors: 50% is half, 25% is a quarter, 10% moves the decimal point one place left, 5% is half of 10%, 1% moves it two places left.
2. Show image I2, then let the student fill the table row by row, easiest column (100) first.
3. For the 75/90/70/55 challenge, the student says a recipe (for example 55% is 50% + 5%) before computing.

Textbook text (verbatim):
Example 3: The maximum marks in a test are 75. If students score 80% or above in the test, they get an A grade. How much should Zubin score at least to get an A grade?
We can find 80% of 75 in different ways, using our understanding of fraction and decimal multiplication, as well as of proportionality.
Fraction Multiplication → 80/100 × 75 = 4/5 × 75 = 60.
Decimal Multiplication → 0.8 × 75 = 60.
Proportional Reasoning → Out of 100, the minimum mark is 80. Out of 75, it is 75 × 80/100 = 60.
(Bar: 0, 15, 30, 45, 60, 75 ↔ 0, 0.2 (20%), 0.4 (40%), 0.6 (60%), 0.8 (80%), 1.0 (100%); “Minimum marks for A grade”, “Total marks”)
Example 4: To prepare a particular millet kanji (porridge), suppose the ratio of millet to water to be mixed for boiling is 2:7. What percentage does the millet constitute in this mixture? If 500 ml of the mixture is to be made, how much millet should be used?
This situation can be modelled as shown in the bar model on the right side.
The ratio of millet to the volume of the mixture is 2:9. In other words, in one unit of the mixture, millet occupies 2/9 units and water occupies 7/9 units.
Estimate first what percentage 2/9 would be.
(Estimation bubbles) Half of 9 is 4.5. So, 2 is clearly less than 50%. Half of 4.5 is 2.25. So, 2/9 is less than 25%. - 10% of 9 is 0.9. 20% of 9 is 1.8. So, 2/9 could be between 20% - 25%.
The percentage (i.e., in 100 such units) of millet in the mixture is 2/9 × 100 = 22.22%.
The percentage of water in the mixture will be 100 - 22.22 = 77.78%.
A mixture with 22.22% millet means 100 ml mixture will have 22.22 ml millet.
Therefore, 500 ml with 22.22% millet will have 5 × 22.22 = 111.1 ml of millet.
A given ratio can be converted to a fraction, and then to a percentage.
The practice of estimating first before calculating can improve number sense and help reduce mistakes. Often, we may not need exact values. The ability to make quick estimates is useful at these times.
Note to the Teacher: Incorporate the practice of estimating before calculating or solving as part of the problem-solving process. You may remind and encourage students as needed.

Textbook text (verbatim):
Example 5: A cyclist cycles from Delhi to Agra and completes 40% of the journey. If he has covered 92 km, how many more kilometres does he have to travel to reach Agra?
Let us first try to model this situation by a bar model. (Bar: Delhi  - 92 km (40%) -  ? - Agra (100%))
Estimate first before solving further.
A few ways of solving this problem are shown below. Does your method match any of the given ones? Do you like any of the other methods?
It is given that 40% of the distance is 92 km. We have to find out how much the rest of the 60% distance is.
Method 1: 40% is 92 km, therefore 20% is 46 km. This makes 60% to be 92 + 46 = 138 km.
Method 2: If 40% is 92, 60% is ? 40 : 92 :: 60 : ? 40/92 = 60/r (r is the remaining distance) r = 60 × 92/40 = 138.
Method 3: 40/100 = 92/d (d is the total distance) d = 92 × 100/40 = 230. Remaining distance = 230 km - 92 km = 138 km.
Method 4: If x is the remaining distance then the total distance from Delhi to Agra is x + 92. Since, we know that 92 is 40% of this total distance, 40/100 × (x + 92) = 92. (x + 92) = 92 × 100/40 x = 230 - 92 = 138.
Drawing rough diagrams can help understand the given situation better and make it easier to think further about the problem.

Textbook text (verbatim):
Percentages Greater than 100
Till now, we saw percentages with a value 100 or less than 100. Can there be percentages with a value more than 100? What could it mean when a percentage is greater than 100? Let us explore.
Example 6: Kishanlal recently opened a garment shop. He aims to achieve a daily sales of at least ₹5000. The sales on the first 2 days were ₹2000 and ₹3500. What percentage of his target did he achieve?
The percentage target achieved is visualised below.
(Day 1: 2000 of 5000 → % of target: 2000/5000 × 100 = 40%; 40% = 40/100 = 2/5 = 0.4. Day 2: 3500 of 5000 → 3500/5000 × 100 = 70%; 70% = 70/100 = 7/10 = 0.7)
It is 40% on Day 1 and 70% on Day 2.
Another way of saying it is - he was 60% short of his target on Day 1 and 30% short of his target on Day 2.
In the next two days, he made ₹5000 and ₹6000 respectively. What percentage of his target are these values?
His target is ₹5000, and he made ₹5000 on Day 3 - this is 100%. On Day 4, he made ₹6000, which is 1000 more than his target.
What percentage of the target was achieved on Day 4?
(Day 3: 5000/5000 × 100 = 100%; 100% = 100/100 = 1/1 = 1.0. Day 4: 6000/5000 × 100 = 120%; 120% = 120/100 = 6/5 = 1.2)
1000 is 20% of 5000. Therefore, 6000, (5000 + 1000) is 100% + 20% = 120% of 5000. It can also be computed as 6000/5000 × 100 = 6/5 × 100 = 120%.
This means he achieved 120% of his target, i.e., 20% more than his target.
On Days 5 and 6 his sales were ₹7800 and ₹9550 respectively. Calculate the percentage of the target achieved on these days.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students calculate the sugar Madhu and Madhav ate from 25% of 120 g and 35% of 95 g, and explain why a percentage alone cannot compare amounts taken from different wholes.
Students build 25%, 10%, 20%, 5%, 40% and 15% of numbers mentally from the blocks 50%, 10%, 5% and 1%, and describe recipes for 75%, 90%, 70% and 55%.
Students complete the fraction, decimal and percentage table, use 0.1 to find 10% of a quantity, and estimate a/b as a percentage to within 5 percentage points.
Students find a percentage of a whole in word problems, such as 80% of 75 marks, and convert a 2 : 7 ratio into a part-of-whole percentage after naming the whole.
Students find the whole from a given part by first finding one piece, such as 20% of the trip from 40% being 92 km, and then find the remaining 138 km.
Students interpret percentages above 100 as more than the whole, find 156%, 191% and 250% from sales and harvests, and write such percentages as fractions and decimals.

video_script.design: One idea: a percent becomes a decimal by reading it as hundredths. Assumes: 1/2 = 0.5, moving the point for ten percent. Wrong idea: to multiply by ten. video_script.wrong_move: A common slip is to multiply 460 rupees by 10 and get 4600 rupees, ten times the whole amount; a part cannot be bigger than the whole, so the slip card is struck.

correct: 0.1 x 460 = 46 rupees is the answer; the decimal point of 460.0 moves one place left to 46.0

video_script.anchor: How much millet in 500 ml of kanji?
video_script.design: One idea: the percentage is of the whole jug. Assumes: millet is 2/9 of the kanji, restated in the hook. Wrong idea: to turn the percent straight into millilitres. Transitions: the 500 ml jug stays on the stage from the hook to the idea part; the nine part lines are drawn in the ground and stay; one clear, before the recap. The Teaching Flow's estimate '500 divided by 9 is about 55.6, double it' is said as 'a little over fifty-five and a half, two parts make about one hundred and eleven', so the doubled rounding never shows 111.2.
video_script.wrong_move: A common slip is to read 22.22% as 22.22 ml and pour that much; a 100 ml mark on the jug shows that pour covers only the first 100 ml, and the jug holds five such hundreds, so the pour is struck through
maths_rules: from the first part of the millet question: millet : water = 2 : 7, the whole is 9 parts, millet = 2/9 = 22.22% (exactly 200/9 %)
the jug holds 500 ml and is drawn split into 9 equal parts; 500 / 9 = 55.555... ml per part, a little over 55 and a half
millet fills 2 parts: 2 x 500 / 9 = 1000/9 = 111.11... ml, about 111 ml
the book's way: 22.22% means 22.22 ml of millet in every 100 ml of kanji; 500 ml is 5 lots of 100 ml; 5 x 22.22 = 111.1 ml
the slip: he pours 22.22 ml, which is the millet for only 100 ml of kanji, one fifth of the jug
check: water fills 7 parts: 7 x 500 / 9 = 388.88... ml, about 389 ml; 500 - 111.1 = 388.9; millet and water together make 500 ml
your turn: a paint mixture is red to yellow 1 : 3; the whole is 4 parts; red in 400 ml is 400 / 4 = 100 ml, never shown
video_script.payoff_line: Use about one hundred and eleven point one millilitres of millet

final_answer.spoken: about one hundred and eleven point one millilitres of millet

video_script.substitution: The 500 ml jug is the whole: split it into nine equal parts, and millet fills two of them.

media.teaching_notes: One idea: the percentage is taken of the whole jug, 500 ml, not of 100. Watch for the slip of turning 22.22% straight into 22.22 ml; ask what the 100% is here. Praise estimating with the fraction 2/9 before any decimal work.

video_script.design: One idea: measure against the target, and one percent of it is a handy block. It assumes finding a percent of a target. The wrong idea is dividing by a hundred, which measures against ten thousand. Transitions: the tube with its target line and 200% tick stays all video; the two day levels are drawn side by side as two tubes. One clear, of the slip bubble, after the break.

maths_rules: both lie between 100% and 200% because 5000 < 7800 < 9550 < 10,000
the slip: 7800 / 100 = 78, which is 7800 out of 10,000, not out of 5000; 78% would sit below the target line
the tube is drawn with the target line at 40% of its height and a faint 200% tick at 80% of its height; liquid height is in proportion to the rupees
video_script.payoff_line: Day five is a hundred and fifty-six percent, and day six is a hundred and ninety-one percent.

final_answer.spoken: a hundred and fifty-six percent and a hundred and ninety-one percent

video_script.substitution: One percent of five thousand rupees is fifty rupees, so count the fifties.

media.teaching_notes: Both answers must sit between one hundred and two hundred percent, because both days are past the target but short of double it. Watch for the slip of knocking two zeros off the rupees, which measures against ten thousand instead of the target.

<bookmark mark='f5'/>Three hundred and fifty-eight over a hundred, halving both, is one hundred and seventy-nine over fifty.
<bookmark mark='f6'/>Twenty-eight point nine over a hundred is two hundred and eighty-nine over one thousand.
<bookmark mark='f7'/>Three hundred and five over a hundred is sixty-one over twenty.

video_script.anchor: Write each percentage as a fraction and a decimal, then mark it on the line.
video_script.design: One idea: a percent, even past a hundred, is a number over a hundred, so its fraction and decimal follow. It assumes dividing by a hundred. The wrong idea is moving the point one place. Transitions: the table stays on the stage all video and fills row by row; the number line arrives in the last idea beat under the table; one clear, of the slip bubble, after the break. The Teaching Flow's order is kept: decimals first, then fractions, then the check. Its word 'easy' and 'just' are dropped.
never_show: 2.89 as an answer outside the wrong struck bubble
video_script.wrong_move: A common slip is to move the point one place and write twenty-eight point nine percent as two point eight nine; the check breaks it, because a percent under a hundred must give a decimal under one.
maths_rules: percent means out of 100: p% = p/100, and the decimal is p / 100, the point moved two places left
173% = 173/100, which cannot be simplified because 173 is prime and shares no factor with 100; decimal 1.73
the slip: 28.9 / 10 = 2.89, the point moved one place; 28.9% < 100% so its decimal must be < 1
the number line runs from 0 (0%) to 4 (400%) with equal gaps; each value is marked at its decimal: 0.15, 0.289, 0.9, 1.1, 1.73, 2, 2.5, 3.05, 3.58
video_script.payoff_line: Twenty-eight point nine percent is nought point two eight nine.

final_answer.spoken: nine over ten and nought point nine, through to sixty-one over twenty and three point zero five

video_script.substitution: Percent means out of a hundred, so put it over a hundred, and dividing by a hundred moves the point two places left.

media.teaching_notes: The quick check for every row: a percent above a hundred gives a decimal above one, and a percent below a hundred gives a decimal below one. Watch for moving the point only one place, which turns twenty-eight point nine percent into two point eight nine.

video_script.anchor: Find the missing numbers in the bars.
video_script.design: One idea: the size of a cell depends on how many cells share the whole. It assumes sharing a number equally. The wrong idea is reusing twenty percent a cell. Transitions: the three pairs of bars stay on the stage all video, each pair lighting up in turn; one clear of the slip bubble after the break. The Teaching Flow's order is kept: read the worked pair first, then the second and third.
never_show: 200% as a real value for the ten-cell bar
120 as the value of six cells
video_script.wrong_move: A common slip is to carry the first bar's twenty percent a cell into the ten-cell bar; ten cells of twenty percent would make two hundred percent, two whole bars, so the picture shows the bar would need to be twice as long.
maths_rules: pair (i), given: 5 equal cells, one cell = 100% / 5 = 20%; whole 75, one cell = 75 / 5 = 15, 4 cells = 4 x 15 = 60
pair (ii): 10 equal cells, one cell = 100% / 10 = 10%; whole 90, one cell = 90 / 10 = 9, 6 cells = 6 x 9 = 54
pair (iii): 4 equal cells, one cell = 100% / 4 = 25%; whole 140, one cell = 140 / 4 = 35, 3 cells = 3 x 35 = 105
checks: 10 x 9 = 90; 4 x 35 = 140; 54 < 90 and 105 < 140 because a part is less than the whole
the slip: 10 cells x 20% = 200%, which is two whole bars
every bar in a pair is drawn the same length; its cells are equal
video_script.payoff_line: Six cells are worth fifty-four, and three cells are worth a hundred and five.

final_answer.value: (ii) one cell 10%, 6 cells = 54; (iii) one cell 25%, 3 cells = 105
final_answer.spoken: ten percent a cell and fifty-four, then twenty-five percent a cell and a hundred and five

video_script.substitution: Count the cells to get one cell's percent, share the whole by the number of cells, then count up.

video_script.anchor: Find each one, and draw its bar.
video_script.design: One idea: the number after 'of' is the whole; choose the quickest route for each percent. Assumes: 10% and 1% blocks, and a quarter as 25%. Wrong idea: to turn decimal minutes into seconds by moving the point. Transitions: the six question rows stay on the stage all video, and each row gets its bar in turn; one clear, before the recap. The Teaching Flow's 'watch me pick the easy route' becomes 'the quickest route', since 'easy' is banned.
video_script.wrong_move: A common slip is to find 1% of an hour as 0.6 minutes and call it 6 seconds; a clock face shows a minute is 60 seconds, not 100, so 0.6 of a minute is far more than 6 seconds, and the 6 seconds is struck through
maths_rules: (i) 25% = 1/4; 160 / 4 = 40; bar of 160 cut into 4 equal parts, 1 part shaded
(iv) 140% of 40 = 100% of 40 + 40% of 40 = 40 + 16 = 56; the bar runs past the 100% mark by 40% of its length
(v) 1 hour = 60 minutes; 1% of 60 minutes = 0.6 minutes; 0.6 x 60 seconds = 36 seconds
the slip: reading 0.6 minutes as 6 seconds, as if a minute had 100 seconds
every bar is drawn to scale inside its own row: the whole is the full bar marked 100%, the shaded part is the percent's share of that length
video_script.payoff_line: In order, forty, forty, two hundred and twenty-three point two, fifty-six, thirty-six seconds, seven hundred grams

final_answer.spoken: forty, forty, two hundred and twenty-three point two, fifty-six, thirty-six seconds, seven hundred grams

video_script.substitution: The number after 'of' is the whole, the full bar; pick a friendly fraction or 10% and 1% blocks to cut it.

media.teaching_notes: One idea: the number after 'of' is the whole, and the quickest route depends on the percent. Watch for the time slip, reading 0.6 of a minute as 6 seconds; a minute has 60 seconds, not 100.

video_script.anchor: Less than, greater than, or equal?
video_script.design: One idea: two numbers decide the size, the percent and the whole. Assumes: finding 10% and 50%. Wrong idea: to trust the bigger whole alone. Transitions: the six rows and their bars stay on the stage all video; each box fills in turn in the idea part; one clear, before the recap. The Teaching Flow's 'left' and 'right' calls are said as 'less than' and 'greater than' so they match the boxes.
never_show: the right bar being longer in pair five
video_script.wrong_move: In pair five a common slip looks only at the wholes, 490 against 200, and says the right side wins; 10% is one tenth and 45% is nearly half, and the left bar is longer, so the call is struck through
maths_rules: (i) 50% of 510 = 255; 50% of 515 = 257.5; same percent, bigger whole on the right; 255 < 257.5, so <
(ii) 37% of 148 = 54.76; 73% of 148 = 108.04; same whole, bigger percent on the right, so <
(iii) 29% of 43 = 12.47; 92% of 110 = 101.2; percent and whole both bigger on the right, so <
(iv) 30% of 40 = 12; 40% of 50 = 20; 12 < 20, so < (both are also bigger on the right)
(vi) 30% of 80 = 24; 24% of 64 = 15.36, about 15; percent and whole both bigger on the left; 24 > 15.36, so >
each row has a small pair of bars; it tips down on the side with the bigger amount; the tilt is the same fixed angle every time and is not drawn to scale
the slip: in pair five it compares only 490 and 200 and calls the right side bigger
video_script.payoff_line: Less than four times, then greater than twice

final_answer.spoken: less than, less than, less than, less than, greater than, greater than

video_script.substitution: Look at two things, the percent and the whole: if one is the same, the other decides; if both are bigger on one side, that side wins.

media.teaching_notes: One idea: the size of a percentage depends on both the percent and the whole. Watch for trusting one number alone, the bigger whole or the bigger percent; the last two pairs flip the pattern of the first four, so ask the student to look at every pair.

MATHEMATICAL IMAGE REQUIREMENT
Teaching purpose: Percentages turn packs of different sizes into bars of the same length, so their ingredient shares can be compared directly.

Composition: Flat, friendly educational illustration for a middle-school maths lesson: plain white background, thin uniform dark outlines (#2B2B2B), flat fills with no shading and no gradients, clean sans-serif labels in plain classroom English a child can read aloud. Colour-blind-safe colours: teal #0072B2 for the first set, amber #E69F00 for the second set, green #009E73 for what agrees or works, reddish purple #CC79A7 for the focus, grey #6B7280 for construction; muted red #D55E00 only for a wrong or impossible case, never as decoration. 16:9 landscape, 1456 by 816 pixels. Two horizontal 100%-stacked bars of exactly the same length, one above the other, left-aligned. The upper bar is labelled 'DEF' with '150 g' beside it; the lower bar is labelled 'Zacni' with '400 g' beside it. Each bar is split, left to right, into four segments: sugar in brown, milk solids in cream with a dark outline, badam in green, food chemicals in grey, with each segment's percentage printed inside it. A small legend names the four colours. A note sits above the bars. Callouts on the right: one linking the two badam segments, one linking the two food chemicals segments, and a large arrow pointing at both sugar segments.

Exact mathematical structure:
- Exactly 2 bars of exactly the same length.
- DEF segments, left to right: 66%, 20%, 8%, 6%.
- Zacni segments, left to right: 68%, 16%, 10%, 6%.
- Segment lengths are proportional to the printed percentages, and each bar's segments add to 100%.
- The two food chemicals segments are exactly equal in length.
- Colours: sugar brown, milk solids cream, badam green, food chemicals grey, the same in both bars.

Visible text:

Critical rejection conditions:
- bars of different lengths, or bars drawn in proportion to the pack weights
- segment lengths that do not match the printed percentages

Wrong idea: to divide by the new price (M2); the idea part also meets M6 with the book's population question. Transitions: the anchor stays all video; the tomato heap and the Rs 30 bar stay from hook to idea; one clear before the theatre (the tomato working moves to a side note), one clear before the recap. The Teaching Flow reads the three cards aloud in its hook; here they are shown but not read, so the tempting 29% is first said by the voice line and 40% is not spoken before the idea.

percentage increase = rise / original price x 100 = 12/30 x 100 = 40%; 12/30 = 2/5 = 0.4
the three answer cards read 12%, 40% and 29%; none is ticked before the idea part

The population question: p is the population in 1961 and q in 1991; statement A: q = 165% of p = 165/100 x p = 1.65p; statement B: q = p + 65% of p = p + 0.65p = 1.65p; so the two statements say the same thing

media.title: Before & After
media.context: Class 8 'Fractions in Disguise', 1.3. The tool for one idea of the topic 'Using Percentages to Compare and to Measure Change': the base of a percentage change is the starting value. Teaching Flow v3, Pattern A (AI drives every step): the AI controls everything; nothing on screen moves unless the AI moves it. PLACEHOLDER: the tool is specified but not built yet; its url is reserved.
media.description:
Two cardboard price tags with a string and a punched hole hang from a clothes rail at the top of the screen. The left tag reads BEFORE, Rs 30, and the right tag reads AFTER, Rs 42, for 1 kg of tomatoes three years apart. Below them lies a single measuring bar with a caption that always says in words which price is being measured against. A small amber flag, '100% is here', clips to one tag at a time. The AI moves the flag and nothing is clickable, so the student chooses, tells and answers.

Before anything is drawn, the student chooses whether the price went up by 12%, 40% or 29%. The AI clips the flag onto BEFORE, so the bar is as long as Rs 30, and attaches the extra Rs 12 as a separate stub on its end. The student says what part of 30 the 12 is, two fifths, and the stub reads 40%. Then the flag unclips, travels across and clips onto AFTER. The bar stretches to Rs 42, the stub keeps exactly the same size, and its reading changes to 28.6%. The same Rs 12 gives a different answer only because the flag moved. The AI asks which flag position the question 'increased from Rs 30' wants, and the student answers BEFORE.

The next case is a fall: theatre footfall going from 160 to 100. Because AFTER is smaller, the change is drawn as an orange notch cut out of the bar instead of a stub added to it. The student says where the flag goes, on 160, and what the decrease is, 37.5%. Last, a population p grows by 65%, drawn as a 100% bar with a 65% stub, and a Relabel toggle redraws the whole thing as one block labelled 165%, so 'increased by 65%' and '165% of the original' are seen to be the same object. Hints come in order. First: what was the price before the change? That is your 100%. Then: the change is new minus old, so what percent of the old price is that? A retry follows with a bus fare going from Rs 40 to Rs 50, which should give 25%. The student learns that a change is always measured against where it started, and that moving the 100% moves the answer.

screen: Top of screen: a horizontal rail, like a clothes rail, with two tags hanging from it. Left tag reads BEFORE with its value (₹30). Right tag reads AFTER with its value (₹42). The tags are drawn as real cardboard price tags with a string and a punched hole.

The flag: a small amber pennant labelled "100% is here", clipped to one tag at a time. When the AI moves it, it visibly unclips, travels across, and clips onto the other tag over 400 ms. This movement is the most important animation in the whole tool.
Middle: a single horizontal measuring bar. Its full length always equals whichever tag holds the flag. When the flag moves, the bar visibly re-scales, it stretches or shrinks to match the new base.

The change stub: the difference (₹12) is drawn as a separate small block in `part`, attached to the end of the bar. Its physical size never changes when the flag moves, only the bar beneath it does. Under the stub, its percentage reading updates: 40% when the flag is on BEFORE, 28.6% when on AFTER.
A caption line under the bar always states in words which base is active: "Measuring against ₹30 (the before price)."
Decrease mode: when AFTER is smaller, the stub is drawn as a notch cut out of the bar in `bad-soft` rather than added on, so falls and rises look different at a glance.
Relabel mode: a toggle redraws the whole bar-plus-stub as one block labelled 165% instead of "100% + 65%", to show they are the same object.
Nothing is clickable.
tool_config.metaphor: two price tags hanging on a shop rail, and a little flag you can clip to one of them to say "measure from here".
tool_config.one_idea: the base of a percentage change is the starting value.

placement.where: on its concept, after the concept video: the AI drives every step and speaks while it moves; the student watches, predicts and answers

tool_config.why_a_tool: moving the flag and watching the same ₹12 report two different percentages is the entire lesson. No still picture can show one quantity changing its answer.
teaching_steps: AI hangs ₹30 on BEFORE and ₹42 on AFTER. "Tomatoes, before and after."
AI plants the flag on BEFORE. "The question says 'from thirty rupees'. So thirty is our hundred percent. The flag goes here."
AI draws the bar to match ₹30, then adds the extra ₹12 as a stub. "Here is the thirty. And here is the extra twelve sticking out."
AI asks: "Twelve is what part of thirty?" (waits) "A bit less than half… it is two-fifths. Forty percent."

AI now drags the flag to AFTER. "Watch what happens if I move the hundred percent to forty-two instead." The bar redraws; the same ₹12 stub now reads 28.6%. "Same twelve rupees. Different answer. Nothing changed except where I put the flag."
AI asks the key question: "So which flag position does the question want, 'from thirty' or 'from forty-two'?" (student answers) "From thirty. Forty percent."
AI repeats with the theatre: 160 to 100, flag on 160. "Your turn. Where does the flag go, and what is the answer?" (37.5% decrease)
AI shows a population p, adds a 65% stub, then relabels the whole thing 165%. "One bar, two labels. Up by sixty-five, or a hundred sixty-five percent of the original. Identical."

tool_config.production_notes: Designed at 1280 x 720, reflowing to 360 px on a phone. Value changes animate over 300 ms ease-out. Full keyboard control, ARIA labels naming current values, 44 px minimum touch targets, WCAG AA contrast. No timers, no scores, no buzzers.

MATHEMATICAL IMAGE REQUIREMENT
Teaching purpose: A percentage change is measured against the original amount, so the ₹12 rise in the tomato price is 40% of the old price.

Composition: Flat, friendly educational illustration for a middle-school maths lesson: plain white background, thin uniform dark outlines (#2B2B2B), flat fills with no shading and no gradients, clean sans-serif labels in plain classroom English a child can read aloud. Colour-blind-safe colours: teal #0072B2 for the first set, amber #E69F00 for the second set, green #009E73 for what agrees or works, reddish purple #CC79A7 for the focus, grey #6B7280 for construction; muted red #D55E00 only for a wrong or impossible case, never as decoration. 16:9 landscape, 1456 by 816 pixels. Two horizontal bars on one rupee scale, one above the other, left-aligned at 0. Upper bar: a teal block labelled 'Old price ₹30' and '100%', followed by an amber stub labelled '+₹12' and '+40%', with a green tick beside it and the caption 'Base: old price'. Lower bar: a single grey block of the same total length as the upper bar, labelled 'New price ₹42' and '100%', with the last ₹12 section outlined in muted red and labelled '28.6%', and a muted red cross beside it with the caption 'Wrong base'.

Exact mathematical structure:
- Both bars have the same total length, standing for ₹42.
- In the upper bar the teal block is exactly 30 parts and the amber stub exactly 12 parts of the same 42-part length.
- The outlined section of the lower bar is exactly the same length as the amber stub above it.
- Only the upper bar carries a tick; only the lower bar carries a cross.

content.text:
Textbook text (verbatim):
1.3 Using Percentages
To Compare Proportions
Example 1: Eesha scored 42 marks out of 50 on an English test and 70 marks out of 80 in a Science test. Since she lost only 8 marks in English but 10 marks in Science, she thinks she has done better at English. Reema does not agree! She argues that since Eesha has scored more marks in Science, she has done better at Science. Vishu thinks we cannot compare the scores because the maximum marks are different. Who do you think is correct?
If the maximum marks are the same, the comparison becomes easier, isn’t it? For these kinds of comparisons, we need to convert both values to percentages.
English score as a percentage = 42/50 × 100 = 84%
Science score as a percentage = 70/80 × 100 = 87.5%.
The Science score (as a percentage) is higher than the English score (as a percentage). So, we can conclude that Eesha has scored better on the Science test.
Know Your Contents (KYC)
Example 2: Madhu and Madhav recently learnt about the importance of reading labels on processed food before purchase. They are at a shop to buy badam drink mix. They are looking at two products and wondering which has a larger share of badam. Can you figure it out? Which product uses a smaller proportion of food chemicals?
(Labels - DEF Badam Mix Powder: Sugar 99 g, Milk solids 30 g, Badam powder 12 g, Food chemicals 9 g, Total weight 150 g. Zacni Badam Mix: Sugar 272 g, Milk solids 64 g, Badam powder 40 g, Food chemicals 24 g, Total weight 400 g.)
It is easier to compare the proportions of the ingredients if we convert them into percentages. For example,
DEF’s sugar content as a percentage of total weight = 99/150 × 100 = 66%.
Complete this table by calculating the percentages to answer the questions: (rows DEF, Zacni; columns Sugar, Milk Solids, Badam Powder, Food Chemicals; DEF sugar 66% given)
(Speech bubbles) “Maybe they should call it ‘Sugar drink mix’” - “Ya! It is very important to Know Your Contents.” - (sign) “Do KYC!”
Check if the percentages of each product add up to 100.

content.text:
Textbook text (verbatim):
Percentage Increase or Decrease
Percentages are often used to describe the rate of change of quantities. For example,
1. Suppose the price of 1 kg tomatoes 3 years ago was ₹30, and the price now is ₹42. The increase in the price is ₹12.
Percentage increase = amount of increase / original amount or base × 100
= 12/30 × 100 = 40%.
We say the price of tomatoes increased by 40% over the last 3 years.
2. The average footfall in this theater before COVID was 160. Now it is just 100. The decrease in the footfall is 60.
Percentage decrease = amount of decrease / original amount or base × 100
= 60/160 × 100 = 37.5%.
We say the footfall in this theater post-COVID has decreased by 37.5%.
Example 3: Do the following two statements mean the same thing?
(i) The population of this state in 1991 is 165% of that in 1961.
(ii) The population of this state has increased by 65% from 1961 to 1991.
Yes, both mean the same. Suppose p is the population of the state in 1961 and q is the population of the state in 1991.
Statement A implies, q = 165% of p; q = 165/100 × p = 1.65p
Statement B implies, q = p + 65% of p; q = p + 0.65 × p = 1.65p
In other words, the population of the state in 1991 is 1.65 times that in 1961.
