content.text:
Teaching plan (logic first):
1. Key idea: a change is always measured against where you started (the original, the base). Redrawing with the other base shows why the choice matters.
2. Increase and decrease use the same recipe: change ÷ original × 100.
3. Example 3: 165% of and increased by 65% are the same thing because the original 100% is already inside the 165%. Show it on the bar: one 100% block plus a 65% stub.
4. Multiplier link (used heavily in Topics 4 to 6): increase by r% means × (1 + r/100); decrease by r% means × (1 − r/100).

(i) now is 85% of before means 85 now, a fall of only 15%: false

the wholesaler sold the sweater to Kishanlal: the wholesaler's CP = Rs 253, SP = Rs 300, profit = 300 - 253 = Rs 47; in this video the wholesaler's percent is not worked out (it is a separate question)
the CP bar of 300 is drawn as 100%; the SP bar of 430 is drawn 430/300 = 1.4333 times as long, so the stub on top is 130/300 of the CP bar
300 is cut into three equal pieces of 100; one piece = 100/300 = 1/3 = 33.33% (33.333...%)
the remaining 30 of the profit = 30/300 = 10%
the slip: 130/430 x 100 = 30.23%, about 30%; it uses the SP as the base

media.title: Shop Counter
media.context: Class 8 'Fractions in Disguise', 1.3. The tool for one idea of the topic 'Buying, Selling and the Price You Compare Against': the cost price is the line everything is measured from. Teaching Flow v3, Pattern A (AI drives every step): the AI controls everything; nothing on screen moves unless the AI moves it. PLACEHOLDER: the tool is specified but not built yet; its url is reserved.
media.description:
A shop counter is drawn in side view with a wall behind it. Across the wall runs a thick line labelled WHAT I PAID, 100%, Rs 300, at about mid height so there is room above and below it. A ruler at the right has 0% at the line, marks going up at plus 10, 25 and 50 percent and down at minus 10 and minus 25 percent, and a pointer that shows the reading for the current stack of notes and coins on the counter. The AI sets the line and the stack. Nothing is clickable, so the student does the thinking and says each percentage aloud.

The AI first stacks Rs 430, the price Kishanlal got for his sweater, and the stack rises above the line. The part above is green and tagged with its value. The student says how much sticks up, Rs 130, and what that is compared with 300, and the pointer settles at 43.33%. Then the line moves to Rs 253 for the wholesaler, who sold for Rs 300, and the student says where the line goes and what comes out: 18.58%. For Raghu's old rice the line moves to Rs 350 and the stack is only Rs 300. The gap is drawn as a hollow orange hatched space tagged Rs 50, and the pointer drops below zero to a loss of about 14.3%.

Then comes the reverse. The line is hidden as a dashed question mark at an unknown height, and only a Rs 50 stack remains, tagged 'this is 125% of what I paid'. The student works out what Shambhavi paid for a crayon box she sold for Rs 50 at a 25% profit: 125% is Rs 50, so 1% is 0.4 and 100% is Rs 40, and the line appears at Rs 40. A side panel then shows the trap, taking 25% off Rs 50 to get Rs 37.50, with the answer struck through, because the profit was never measured from the selling price. Hints come in order. First: who paid what first? That is the 100%. Then: is the selling price longer or shorter than the cost, and by how much as a part of the cost? If still stuck, a worked example uses cost Rs 80 and selling price Rs 100, which is 25%, followed by a retry with cost Rs 120 and selling price Rs 150. The student learns that profit and loss are one idea measured from the same line, the cost price.

screen: Background: a simple shop counter in side view, with a wall behind it.

The line: a thick horizontal line drawn across the wall, running the full width, labelled at its left end WHAT I PAID · 100% · ₹300. It is the visual anchor of the whole tool and sits at about mid-height so there is room both above and below it.

The money stack: notes and coins stack upward from the counter surface. If the stack rises above the line, the portion above is `good` (green) and tagged with its rupee value. If the stack falls short, the gap between the stack top and the line is drawn as a hollow, hatched space in `bad-soft` (orange) and tagged with the shortfall.
Side scale: a vertical ruler at the right, with 0% at the line itself and marks going up (+10, +25, +50%) and down (−10, −25%). The reading for the current stack appears as a pointer on this scale.

Hide-the-line mode: for reverse questions, the line is drawn as a dashed question mark line at an unknown height, while the stack is fully known and tagged "this is 125% of what I paid". The AI then works downward to place the line. This is the single most valuable state in the tool and must be built.
Trap display: a small side panel can show the wrong method (taking the percentage off the selling price) with its answer struck through in `bad-soft`, for the moment the AI names the trap.
Nothing is clickable.
tool_config.metaphor: a shop counter with a line marked on the wall behind it, the level the shopkeeper has to reach just to get his own money back.
tool_config.one_idea: the cost price is the line everything is measured from.

placement.where: on its concept, after the concept video: the AI drives every step and speaks while it moves; the student watches, predicts and answers

tool_config.why_a_tool: a fixed line with stacks rising above and falling below makes profit and loss one idea instead of two, and the hide-the-line step makes the reverse problem visible rather than algebraic.
ai_controls: hide the line and work backwards
teaching_steps: AI sets the line at ₹300. "This line is what the shopkeeper paid. Three hundred rupees. Everything gets measured from here."
AI stacks ₹430 of notes; the stack rises above the line. "He sold it for four thirty. Look, it clears the line."
AI asks: "How much is sticking up above the line?" (₹130) "And a hundred thirty compared to three hundred is…?" (waits) AI reveals 43.33% on the side scale.
AI resets the line to ₹253, stacks ₹300. "Now the wholesaler. You tell me where the line goes and what comes out." (18.58%)
AI sets the line to ₹350, stacks only ₹300, the stack falls short. "Raghu's rice. The stack does not reach the line. Fifty rupees missing." (14.29% loss)

The reverse, which is the hard one. AI hides the line and shows only a ₹50 stack with a tag "this is 125% of what I paid". "Now work backwards. He sold crayons at fifty rupees and made twenty-five percent profit. What did he pay?"

AI marks the stack: 100% + 25% = 125% = ₹50. "So a hundred and twenty-five percent is fifty rupees. Twenty-five percent is a quarter of that hundred-twenty-five… let me do it cleanly, if a hundred twenty-five percent is fifty, then one percent is nought point four, so a hundred percent is forty." Line appears at ₹40.

AI names the trap: "And the wrong answer people give is fifty minus twenty-five percent of fifty, thirty-seven fifty. That takes the percentage off the selling price. But the profit was never measured from there."

tool_questions.note: Questions are authored when the tool is built; the teaching steps above are the brief.

tool_config.production_notes: Designed at 1280 x 720, reflowing to 360 px on a phone. Value changes animate over 300 ms ease-out. Full keyboard control, ARIA labels naming current values, 44 px minimum touch targets, WCAG AA contrast. No timers, no scores, no buzzers.

media.generation_prompt:
MATHEMATICAL IMAGE REQUIREMENT
Teaching purpose: When the selling price is 125% of the cost price, find one 25% piece first; the cost price is four such pieces.

Composition: Flat, friendly educational illustration for a middle-school maths lesson: plain white background, thin uniform dark outlines (#2B2B2B), flat fills with no shading and no gradients, clean sans-serif labels in plain classroom English a child can read aloud. Colour-blind-safe colours: teal #0072B2 for the first set, amber #E69F00 for the second set, green #009E73 for what agrees or works, reddish purple #CC79A7 for the focus, grey #6B7280 for construction; muted red #D55E00 only for a wrong or impossible case, never as decoration. 16:9 landscape, 1456 by 816 pixels. One long horizontal bar split into 5 equal pieces. The first 4 pieces are teal and are bracketed underneath as 100%, CP ₹40. The 5th piece is amber and marked 25% above it. Each piece carries ₹10 inside. A brace over the whole bar reads 125%, SP ₹50. A small caption at the top left names the crayon box.

Exact mathematical structure:
- Exactly 5 equal pieces in one bar.
- Pieces 1 to 4 teal, piece 5 amber.
- Each piece shows ₹10 inside it.
- Brace over all 5 pieces: 125% and SP ₹50.
- Bracket under pieces 1 to 4: 100% and CP ₹40.
- Label 25% above piece 5 only.

Visible text:
- Crayon box
- ₹10
- 25%
- 125%
- SP ₹50
- 100%
- CP ₹40

Critical rejection conditions:
- the bar has a number of pieces other than 5, or pieces of unequal length
- the 100% bracket covers more or fewer than 4 pieces
- the cost price is shown as ₹50 or the selling price as ₹40
- any count of objects, cells, ticks or dots that differs from the numbers stated above
- any text beyond the listed visible text, or any listed text misspelled or altered
- any board name, publisher name, book title, page number or curriculum branding anywhere in the frame

Student takeaway: ₹50 is 125%, so one 25% piece is ₹10 and the cost price is ₹40.

video_script.anchor: What percent did Raghu lose on his rice?
video_script.design: One idea: a loss percent is measured against the cost price, and the share stays the same for one kilo or ten. It assumes the profit percent from Kishanlal's sweater question. The wrong idea (M2) is a common slip: he divides by what Raghu got back, and the picture shows that three hundred is the short stack, not the cost bar. Transitions: the anchor stays all video; the store shrinks to the corner at the ground part; the cost bar and the short stack stay from ground to idea; the one-kilo bar arrives beside the ten-kilo bar; one clear before the recap.
video_script.wrong_move: A common slip is to divide the loss by the selling price, 50 out of 300, and get about 16.67%; the 300 is what Raghu got back, not what he paid, so the base is wrong and the wrong answer is struck through.
maths_rules: Raghu bought rice at Rs 35 a kg; 10 kg cost 10 x 35 = Rs 350 = the cost price = 100%
he sold the 10 kg for Rs 300; loss = 350 - 300 = Rs 50
350 = 7 x 50, so the loss is 50/350 = 1/7 of the cost
1/7 x 100 = 14.2857...% = about 14.29% (the book prints 14.28%, cut off rather than rounded)
one kilo: sold at 300 / 10 = Rs 30 a kg; loss on one kilo = 35 - 30 = Rs 5; 5/35 = 1/7, about 14.29%, the same
the slip: 50/300 x 100 = 16.666...% = about 16.67%; it uses the SP as the base
the SP stack is drawn 300/350 = 6/7 of the cost bar; the gap is 1/7 of the bar
your turn: a shopkeeper buys 20 kg of rice at Rs 25 a kg (cost Rs 500) and sells it all for Rs 400; loss 100; 100/500 x 100 = 20%; never shown
video_script.payoff_line: Raghu's loss is about fourteen point two nine percent of what he paid

final_answer.value: about 14.29%, and the same when worked for one kilo
final_answer.spoken: about fourteen point two nine percent

video_script.substitution: The fifty rupees short is one seventh of the three hundred and fifty he paid, and one kilo gives five out of thirty-five, also one seventh.
video_script.wrong_answer: about sixteen point six seven percent

media.teaching_notes: One idea: a loss is measured against what was paid, exactly like a profit, and a percent does not change with the size of the pile. media.generation_prompt:
MATHEMATICAL IMAGE REQUIREMENT
Teaching purpose: The same ₹250 profit is 50% of the ₹500 cost but only 33.33% of the ₹750 revenue, because the percentage depends on which amount is the 100%.

Composition: Flat, friendly educational illustration for a middle-school maths lesson: plain white background, thin uniform dark outlines (#2B2B2B), flat fills with no shading and no gradients, clean sans-serif labels in plain classroom English a child can read aloud. Colour-blind-safe colours: teal #0072B2 for the first set, amber #E69F00 for the second set, green #009E73 for what agrees or works, reddish purple #CC79A7 for the focus, grey #6B7280 for construction; muted red #D55E00 only for a wrong or impossible case, never as decoration. 16:9 landscape, 1456 by 816 pixels. Two horizontal bars, one above the other, drawn to the same scale and starting at the same left edge. Top bar: a teal block for the cost ₹500 marked 100%, with an amber block ₹250 attached to its right end marked 50%. Bottom bar: one block for the revenue ₹750 marked 100%, with its right-hand ₹250 part shaded amber and marked 33.33%. A short heading sits beside each bar.

Exact mathematical structure:
- Two bars on one shared scale with a common left edge.
- Top bar: teal ₹500 block labelled 100%, plus amber ₹250 block labelled 50%; total length equals the bottom bar.
- Bottom bar: full length ₹750 labelled 100%, with its last ₹250 shaded amber and labelled 33.33%.
- Both amber parts have the same length.
- The ₹500 block is exactly two times the length of the ₹250 block.

Visible text:
- On cost
- On revenue
- ₹500
- ₹750
- ₹250
- 100%
- 50%
- 33.33%

Critical rejection conditions:
- the two amber parts differ in length
- the bars are drawn to different scales
- 50% is placed on the revenue bar or 33.33% on the cost bar
- any count of objects, cells, ticks or dots that differs from the numbers stated above
- any text beyond the listed visible text, or any listed text misspelled or altered
- any board name, publisher name, book title, page number or curriculum branding anywhere in the frame

Student takeaway: The same profit gives a different percentage when the base changes.

narration: Kiko has one question to ask.
What is the real-life use case?
A shopkeeper wants to know how hard his money works.
He finds profit percent on what he paid, because that shows profit for each hundred rupees.
He finds net profit on his monthly sales to see what he keeps.
beats.on_screen: Kiko at bottom right, blue question box beside him with the question, then a stack of fertiliser bags, and a profit block laid on the cost bar Photo: Stacked fertiliser bags in a shop

narration: Kiko has one question to ask.
What mistake do some students make here?
Some students always compare the profit with the bigger number, seven hundred and fifty.
That is wrong for profit percent, because it tells how hard her money worked.
So we measure it on what she paid, five hundred, which gives fifty percent.
beats.on_screen: Kiko at bottom right, blue question box beside him with the question, then the cost bar Rs 500 ticked as the hundred percent and Rs 750 crossed out

video_script.anchor: Bought for 500, sold for 750. What is Manisha's profit percent?
video_script.design: One idea: the same rupees become different percents on different hundreds, so name the hundred. It assumes profit percent on the cost price, and gross and net profit. The wrong idea: the wrong rule of always using the bigger number. The anchor and the profit block stay all video; the cost bar and the revenue bar stay from the ground to the idea; the month's bar arrives in the last idea beat; one clear, before the recap. The Teaching Flow teaches this as a conversation (4.4 steps 1 to 5); the thirty-three percent reading is kept.
video_script.wrong_move: A common slip is to say to always compare the profit with the bigger number, Rs 750; the two bars show that profit percent is measured on what she paid, Rs 500, and that the Rs 750 comparison answers a different question.
maths_rules: Manisha buys a 50 kg bag for Rs 500 and sells it for Rs 750; profit = 750 - 500 = Rs 250
on what she paid: 250 / 500 = 1/2 = 50%
the two bars on one scale: the cost bar is 500 units long, the revenue bar 750 units long; the same 250-unit profit block is half of the first and one third of the second
a month: sales Rs 1,50,000; goods cost Rs 1,00,000; gross profit = 1,50,000 - 1,00,000 = Rs 50,000; other expenses Rs 5,000; net profit = 50,000 - 5,000 = Rs 45,000
net profit percent of the month's revenue = 45,000 / 1,50,000 x 100 = 3/10 x 100 = 30%
the wrong rule 'always the bigger number' is wrong: in this chapter profit percent is measured on the cost price unless the question names another base
your turn: a shopkeeper buys a vase for Rs 400 and sells it for Rs 500; profit Rs 100; 25% on what was paid, 20% on what came in; never shown
video_script.payoff_line: Her profit is fifty percent of what she paid.

final_answer.value: 50% on cost (500); 33.33% on revenue (750); net profit 30% of monthly revenue
final_answer.spoken: fifty percent on what she paid, thirty-three point three three percent on what came in, and a net profit of thirty percent of the month's revenue

video_script.substitution: The same profit laid against a different hundred gives a different percent, so always say which hundred.
video_script.wrong_answer: always compare the profit with the bigger number

media.teaching_notes: The same profit is a different percent on a different hundred: 50% of the cost, 33.33% of the revenue. Neither is wrong, but you must say which. Profit percent in this chapter means on the cost. Watch for 'always use the bigger number'.

content.text:
Textbook text (verbatim):
Profit and Loss
You may have the experience of buying something - snacks, groceries, clothes, toys, etc. Very often, the shopkeeper quotes a price and after some bargaining the customer pays the negotiated amount and buys the item(s). We call the price quoted by the shopkeeper the marked price (sometimes this can be the MRP of an item). The price the customer pays after a discount is called the selling price. Also, the price the shopkeeper paid to purchase that item is called the cost price. Let us see how these labels are relative to the context through an example.
The picture below shows the journey of a sweater from the manufacturer to the customer and what the cost price (CP), the marked price (MP), and the selling price (SP) mean in each step.
(Picture: Manufacturing Unit → Wholesale Store → Retail Store → Customer. Manufacturing unit: CP ₹230, MP ₹255, SP ₹253. Wholesale store: CP ₹253, MP ₹310, SP ₹300. Retail store: CP ₹300, MP ₹480, SP ₹430.)
Kishanlal (retailer) buys sweaters from a wholesaler at a price of ₹300 per sweater. The marked price he quotes his customers is ₹480. After bargaining, he sells this sweater at ₹430. Notice that the selling price is greater than the cost price, resulting in a profit of ₹430 - ₹300 = ₹130. If the selling price is less than the cost price, it will result in a loss.

Example 4: Find out the percentage profit Kishanlal made on this sweater.
We shall consider the cost price to be 100% to find out the percentage profit made with reference to the cost price. The following rough diagram describes this situation.

Teaching plan (logic first):
1. Key idea: profit % and loss % are just percentage change (3.2) with the cost price as the base.
2. Forward (CP known): SP = CP × (1 + profit%), so the notebooks cost 36 × 1.2.
3. Reverse (SP known): SP is 125% of CP, so find one piece (25%) first. This is the 2.5 whole-from-a-part idea again. Never take 25% of the SP (M4).
4. Per-kg question: a percentage does not care about the scale, so 5/35 is the same as 50/350.

Textbook text (verbatim):
Example 6: Shyamala had procured decorative vases at ₹2650 per piece. One of the pieces was slightly damaged. She decides to sell it at a loss of 18%. How much will she get by selling this piece?
Try making an estimate. Draw a rough diagram depicting the given situation.
Two methods of solving this are shown.
(Method A) With respect to the buying price being 100%, the selling price is 18% less than the buying price. That is, the selling price would be 82%. 82% of 2650 = 0.82 × 2650 = 2173.
(Method B) The loss amount is 18% of 2650. That is, 18/100 × 2650 = 477. Reducing this from the buying price, 2650 - 477 = 2173.
The sale amount of the damaged vase would be ₹2173.
Due to heavy rains, Snehal could not transport strawberries to Hyderabad from his farm in Panchgani. He sells some of his stock at ₹80 per kg with a 12% loss. What is the cost price?
You have probably seen percentages mentioned when shops offer discounts! Do you know what 30% off (or 30% discount) means? It means that the shop is willing to reduce the price of the item by 30%.
A utensil store is offering a 35% discount on the cooker with an MRP ₹1800. What is the selling price? If the cost price was ₹900, what is the percentage profit made after the sale?

content.text:
Textbook text (verbatim):
Suppose Kishanlal achieved a sales of ₹80,000 last month. Out of this, the amount he spent on buying these goods he sold last month was ₹48,000. The difference amount, ₹80,000 - ₹48,000 = ₹32,000, is called gross profit.
After deducting the other expenses he incurred (such as transport cost, employee’s salary, electricity bill, etc.) amounting to ₹8,000, the amount remaining is called net profit, which is ₹32,000 - ₹8,000 = ₹24,000.
Note: In this chapter, the term profit refers to gross profit.
Manisha sells fertiliser. She buys 50 kg bags at ₹500 per bag. She sells it at ₹750 per bag making a profit of 250/500 × 100 = 50%.
Although, with respect to the ₹750 amount she has earned by selling a bag, the profit percentage is 250/750 × 100 = 33.33%.
(Bars: 0 - 500 (100%) + 250 (50%); 0 - 750 (100%) with 250 = 33.33%)
Profit percentage is calculated based on the price the goods bought when we want to know “How much profit did I make compared to what I invested in buying the goods?”.
Profit percentage is calculated based on the revenue (sales amount) when we want to know “How much (net) profit did I make on my overall revenue?”.
Suppose, in a month she made sales of ₹1,50,000. The cost of buying the goods was ₹1,00,000. So, the gross profit is ₹50,000. The monthly expenses amounted to ₹5,000. The net profit is ₹45,000. Out of monthly revenue (₹1,50,000), the net profit percentage is 45000/150000 × 100 = 3/10 × 100 = 30%.

content.text:
How the AI teaches this:
1. "Manisha buys a bag of fertiliser for five hundred, sells it for seven fifty. Profit, two hundred fifty rupees. What is her profit percentage?"
2. Student says 50%. "Correct, two fifty on the five hundred she invested."
3. "Now her accountant says it is thirty-three percent. Is the accountant wrong?" (Let them wrestle.)
4. "He is not. He is comparing the two fifty to the seven fifty that came in. Two fifty out of seven fifty is a third. Same rupees. Different question."
5. The distinction, plainly: "Compare to what you paid when you want to know 'how hard did my money work'. Compare to revenue when you want to know 'out of all the money that came in, how much did I keep'."
6. Gross vs net in one line: "Gross profit is sales minus what the goods cost. Net profit is what survives after rent, salaries and electricity too. In this chapter, 'profit' means gross."

content.text:
How the AI teaches this:
1. "Nine percent of four fifty. Ten percent would be forty-five, so nine percent is a bit less, forty and a half. Correct."
2. "Why two nine percents instead of one eighteen? Because the tax is split between the central and the state government. Together it is eighteen percent."
3. "Quick way to check any GST bill: four fifty times one point one eight, five thirty-one. Matches."
4. Send them off with a task: "Find a real bill at home. Check the shop's arithmetic. Shops do get it wrong."

video_script.anchor: What profit percent did the wholesaler make, and the factory?
video_script.design: One idea: each seller's hundred percent is what that seller paid. It assumes a cost-price bar as the hundred percent. The wrong idea (M2) is a common slip: he borrows Kishanlal's three hundred as the wholesaler's base, and the picture shows the three hundred bar belongs to someone else. Transitions: the anchor stays all video; the chain shrinks to a strip at the top at the ground part and stays; the two bars stay through the break and the idea; one clear before the recap.
video_script.wrong_move: A common slip is to measure the wholesaler's profit of 47 against 300, Kishanlal's cost price, and get about 16%; the 300 bar is Kishanlal's, while the wholesaler's own bar is 253, so the wrong answer is struck through.
maths_rules: the chain: the factory's CP = Rs 230, it sells to the wholesaler at Rs 253; the wholesaler's CP = Rs 253, it sells to Kishanlal at Rs 300; Kishanlal's CP = Rs 300
wholesaler: profit = 300 - 253 = Rs 47; bar of 253 = 100%
10% of 253 = 25.3; 20% of 253 = 50.6; 47 is a little less than 50.6, so the answer is a little under 20%
factory: profit = 253 - 230 = Rs 23; 10% of 230 = 23; 23/230 x 100 = 10% exactly
the slip: 47/300 x 100 = 15.67%, about 16%; it uses Kishanlal's cost price, not the wholesaler's
the two stubs compared at the end: wholesaler about 18.58%, factory 10%
every bar is drawn to scale from its own cost price; the stubs are 130/300, 47/253 and 23/230 of their bars

video_script.anchor: What is the profit margin on the geometry box, compared with the cost?
video_script.design: One idea: profit margin on cost is the profit as a share of what was paid, and an estimate guards the answer. It assumes the profit percent from Kishanlal's sweater question. The wrong idea (M2) is a common slip: dividing by the selling price. Transitions: the anchor stays all video; the shop shrinks to the corner at the ground part; the cost bar stays from ground to idea; one clear before the recap.
video_script.wrong_move: A common slip is to divide the profit by the selling price, 35 out of 110, and get about 32%; 110 is what the student paid, not the shopkeeper, so the base is wrong and the wrong answer is struck through.
maths_rules: cost price = Rs 75 = 100%; selling price = Rs 110
profit = 110 - 75 = Rs 35
35/75: divide top and bottom by 5 to get 7/15
7/15 is a bit under 1/2, because half of 15 is 7.5; so the answer is a bit under 50%
check: 46.67% of 75 = 0.4667 x 75 = 35.0025, about 35, which is the profit (exactly 7/15 x 75 = 35)
the slip: 35/110 x 100 = 31.8%, about 32%; it uses the selling price as the base
the profit stub on the cost bar is drawn 35/75 = 7/15 of the bar, a little under half of it
video_script.payoff_line: The profit margin is about forty-six point six seven percent

final_answer.spoken: about forty-six point six seven percent

video_script.substitution: The profit of thirty-five rupees is compared with the seventy-five paid, which is seven fifteenths, a bit under half.

media.teaching_notes: One idea: profit margin on cost is the profit over the cost price; estimate first (seven fifteenths is a bit under half). Watch for M2, dividing by the selling price (35 out of 110, about 32%).

video_script.design: One idea: the profit is added on top of the cost, so a fifty percent margin means one and a half times the cost. It assumes halving a number. profit margin 50% means the profit is 50% of the cost = half of 475
half of 400 = 200; half of 75 = 37.50; half of 475 = 237.50
selling price = 475 + 237.50 = Rs 712.50
check: 712.50 - 475 = 237.50, and 237.50 x 2 = 475, so the profit is exactly half of the cost
the slip: he calls the profit, Rs 237.50, the price; 237.50 is less than 475, so the chair would be sold at a loss
the selling bar is drawn 1.5 times the cost bar; the wrong bar is drawn 0.5 times the cost bar

the other candidates share 1600 - 500 = 1100 votes; each of them must get fewer than 500, or the winner would not have won

3 candidates in all: two others share 1100, so one of them gets at least 1100 / 2 = 550, more than 500, so no
4 candidates in all: three others can get 499, 499 and 102; 499 + 499 + 102 = 1100, and each is under 500, so yes
the smallest number of candidates is 4
the winner's share, 31.25%, is less than one third (33.33...%)
the vote bars are drawn to one scale: 500 units for the winner, and the others' bars sum to 1100 units

video_script.anchor: Two buffaloes, eighty thousand rupees each: overall gain or loss?
video_script.design: One idea: equal percentages on unequal bases never cancel, so find each cost first. It assumes the backwards move (a price is 105 percent or 90 percent of the cost). The wrong idea: to take five from ten. The anchor and the two cost bars stay from the ground to the recap; the working band clears once, before the recap. Following the Teaching Flow, the visuals are two separate cost bars side by side, because the whole difficulty is that the two animals had different costs.
video_script.wrong_move: A common slip is to take five from ten and say he loses five percent overall; the two cost bars appear with different lengths, so the five percent and the ten percent are parts of different wholes and cannot be taken from each other.
maths_rules: each buffalo sold for Rs 80,000; total received = 2 x 80,000 = Rs 1,60,000
first buffalo: 5% profit on its cost, so 80,000 = 105% of its cost; cost = 80,000 / 1.05 = 76,190.48..., about Rs 76,190
second buffalo: 10% loss on its cost, so 80,000 = 90% of its cost; cost = 80,000 / 0.9 = 88,888.89..., about Rs 88,889
loss percent on what he paid = 5,079.37 / 1,65,079.37 x 100 = 3.0769..., about 3.08%
the profit on the first is about Rs 3,810; the loss on the second is about Rs 8,889; 8,889 - 3,810 = 5,079
the wrong move: 10% - 5% = 5% loss; 5% of 1,60,000 = Rs 8,000, which is not the loss
the two cost bars are drawn on one scale: the first 76,190 units long, the second 88,889 units long, so the second is about 1.17 times as long; the Rs 80,000 mark is at the same height on both
video_script.payoff_line: He loses about five thousand and seventy-nine rupees.

final_answer.spoken: a loss of about five thousand and seventy-nine rupees, about three point zero eight percent

video_script.substitution: Find what each buffalo cost first, because each percentage is measured on its own cost.

the principal is Rs 6000, the money put in; it is the 100% of the bar
interest after 1 year = 10% of 6000 = 0.10 x 6000 = Rs 600; the 10% stub is drawn one tenth as long as the 6000 bar
amount after 1 year = 6000 + 600 = Rs 6600
the wrong idea that only the interest comes back is wrong for an FD: at the end of the term both the deposit and the interest are returned

media.title: Two Jars
media.context: Class 8 'Fractions in Disguise', 1.3. The tool for one idea of the topic 'Money That Grows, and Money That Shrinks': Interest left in the jar starts earning too. Teaching Flow v3, Pattern B (student explores, AI stays quiet): the student controls everything; the AI does not teach here. It is used again on M4.S14.T14.C142. PLACEHOLDER: the tool is specified but not built yet; its url is reserved.
media.description:
Two glass savings jars stand side by side on a shelf, the left one labelled TAKEN OUT and the right one LEFT IN, both starting at the same coin level. Below them are a table with columns Year, Start, Interest this year and End for each jar, and a graph of amount against years. The student has the controls: principal from Rs 100 to Rs 1,00,000, rate from 1 to 20 percent, years from 1 to 30, a Next year button, a Run button, a Reset and a Growth or Decline switch. The AI says one line, 'now go and break it', and then stays quiet.

The student begins with Rs 6000 at 10 percent and presses Next year. In the left jar the coin level never rises, because a handful of coins leaves each year and drops into a purse labelled 'Taken home so far', reaching Rs 1800 after 3 years, so Rs 7800 in all. In the right jar each year's interest settles in amber on top of the blue coins, and the amber band is thicker every year, Rs 600, Rs 660, then Rs 726, with a dashed line marking last year's level and a small arrow beside each new interest value in the table, ending at Rs 7986. On the graph the taken-out jar is a straight line and the left-in jar is a curve, and the wedge between them is shaded as what compounding gave you. Both jars share one scale, so the comparison is fair.

Then the student explores freely. Run for 20 years. Compare 5 percent for 4 years with 10 percent for 2 years: both are 20 percent in simple interest, yet with the interest left in the 5 percent jar ends higher. Watch where money doubles at 10 percent, in about 7 years with compounding against 10 without. Try to make the two jars end up equal, and notice that the table agrees in year 1 and parts company from year 2. The only nudge, if nothing surprises the student, is whether they tried a long time at a small rate.

In Decline mode there is one jar that shrinks and its coins fade out as they leave. A television worth Rs 21,000 falling 5 percent a year loses Rs 1050 in the first year and a little less, Rs 997.50, in the second. The student learns that interest left in earns interest too, and that decline is the same idea in reverse.

screen: Upper half: two glass jars side by side, drawn with a visible glass edge and a slight shine so they read as containers, not bar charts. Left jar is labelled TAKEN OUT, right jar LEFT IN. Both start with the same coin level.

Left jar behaviour: the coin level never rises. Each year, a small handful of coins animates up and out of the jar and drops into a purse drawn below it. The purse fills across the years and carries a running label: "Taken home so far: ₹1,800".

Right jar behaviour: each year's interest coins drop into the jar in `part` (amber), settling on top of the existing `fill` (blue) coins. The blue never changes; the amber band grows, and each year's amber band is visibly thicker than the last. A faint dashed line marks last year's level so the increment is measurable by eye.
Scale: both jars share one vertical scale, which auto-fits so the taller jar sits at about 85% height. Both jars must always be drawn at the same scale, this is the comparison.
Lower left, the table: columns Year · Start · Interest this year · End, one block per jar, filling one row per year press. In the compounding block, each new interest value gets a small ↑ next to it.

Lower right, the graph: x-axis years, y-axis amount. A straight `fill` line for the taken-out jar, a curving `part` line for the left-in jar. The area between them shades lightly, that shaded wedge is "what compounding gave you".
Controls (the student uses these, not the AI): principal (₹100-₹1,00,000), rate (1 to 20%), years (1 to 30), a Next year button, a Run button, a Reset, and a Growth / Decline switch.
Decline mode: one jar only. It shrinks each year, coins fading out as they leave, and each year's loss is visibly smaller than the last. Table columns become Year · Start · Decrease this year · End.

maths_rules: principal 6000, rate 10% = 10/100 = 0.1 for every year, 3 years
Option one, no compounding: interest each year 6000 x 0.1 = 600; after 3 years 6000 + 600 x 3 = 6000 + 6000 x 0.1 x 3 = 6000 + 1800 = 7800
letters: p = principal (6000), r = rate as a decimal (0.1), t = number of years (3); 1.1 = 1 + r
no compounding: interest one year = p x r; t years = p x r x t; amount = p + p x r x t = p(1 + rt); check: 6000(1 + 0.1 x 3) = 6000 x 1.3 = 7800
compounding: each year multiplies the amount by (1 + r); after t years amount = p x (1 + r) x ... x (1 + r), t times = p(1 + r)^t; check: 6000 x 1.1^3 = 7986
total interest = amount - principal: without compounding p x r x t (6000 x 0.1 x 3 = 1800); with compounding p(1 + r)^t - p (7986 - 6000 = 1986)
the slip: r = 10 gives 6000 x (1 + 10) = 6000 x 11 = 66000 after one year, eleven times the money

content.text:
Textbook text (verbatim):
Growth and Compounding
You might have come across statements like, “1 year interest for FD (Fixed Deposit) in the bank @ 6% per annum” or “Savings account with interest @ 2.5% per annum”. Interest is the extra money paid by institutions like banks or post offices on money deposited (kept) with them. Interest is also paid by people or institutions when they borrow money.
In a Fixed Deposit (FD), you deposit a specific amount of money for a fixed period at a predetermined interest rate. The money remains locked for the chosen duration, and the bank pays you interest on it. You cannot withdraw the amount before the maturity date without incurring a penalty. At the end of the term, you receive both your original deposit and the interest earned.
For example, a bank says that the interest rate for fixed deposits is 10% p.a. What do you understand by this statement? What is the ‘p.a.’ next to the percentage?
‘p.a.’ is the short form of per annum, which means for every year. The specified interest rate indicates that if you invest ₹6000 as a deposit for a year with the bank, they will give you ₹600 as interest on this deposit. The 10% is the rate of interest and the ₹6000 on which the interest is calculated is the principal. The amount after 1 year in your bank account will be
6000 + (0.10 × 6000)
(principal) + (10% interest on principal)
= 6000 + 600 = 6600.
(Bar: 0 - Principal (initial deposit) 100% - +10%; Amount after 1 year)
In other words, the amount deposited, ₹6000, will become 110% (or increase by 10%),
6000 × 110% = 6000 × 110/100 = 6000 × 1.1 = 6600.
This can also be expressed as
Amount after 1 year = Principal (P) + rate of interest (r) of P

content.text:
Textbook text (verbatim):
Example 7: If one deposits ₹6000 in the bank, what is the amount after 3 years?
That depends on the choice of FD. There are two possibilities:
1. Option 1: The interest is paid out regularly (for example, every year). The principal amount is returned after the maturity period.
(Table - Year 1: Beginning ₹6000, × 0.10 → Ending ₹600 returned, Amount in the FD ₹6000; Year 2: Beginning ₹6000 → Ending ₹600 returned, ₹6000; Year 3: Beginning ₹6000 → Ending ₹600 returned, ₹6000. Total amount received ₹1800 + ₹6000 = ₹7800)
2. Option 2: The interest gained every time (say after each year) is added back to the FD, thus increasing the principal amount for the subsequent period. After the maturity period, the entire amount is returned. This phenomenon is called compounding.
(Table - Year 1: Beginning ₹6000, × 0.10 → ₹600 added back, Ending ₹6600 (× 1.10); Year 2: Beginning ₹6600 → ₹660 added back, Ending ₹7260 (× 1.10); Year 3: Beginning ₹7260 → ₹726, Ending ₹7986 (× 1.10); ₹7986 is returned. Total amount received ₹7986)
We can see that with compounding, the final amount is more.
Example 8: What percent is the total amount received with respect to the amount deposited in both the options?
This can be calculated by finding total amount received / amount deposited × 100.
Without Compounding: 7800/6000 × 100 = 130% = 1.3. In other words, the total amount received = 6000 × (1 + 0.1 + 0.1 + 0.1) = 6000 × 1.3. The percentage gain over 3 years is 30%.
With Compounding: 7986/6000 × 100 = 133.1% = 1.331. In other words, the total amount received = 6000 × 1.1 × 1.1 × 1.1. = 6000 × 1.331. The percentage gain over 3 years is 33.1%.

content.text:
Teaching plan (logic first):
1. Key idea: with compounding, last year's interest starts earning interest too. The base grows every year (the base idea again).
2. Without compounding: add 10% of the same 6000 three times, × (1 + 0.1 + 0.1 + 0.1). With compounding: × 1.1 each year, × 1.1 × 1.1 × 1.1.
3. Connect to Power Play: repeated multiplication is exponential growth; repeated addition is linear growth.

content.text:
Textbook text (verbatim):
Let us try to generalise the pattern observed in each of the options.
Example 9: What is the amount we get back if we invest ₹6000 at an interest rate of 10% p.a. for ‘t’ years?
No Compounding
Here, the interest gained every term is paid back. Therefore, the principal amount for every term shall remain the same, and as a result, the interest gained every term also shall be the same.
The interest gained in 1 term is 6000 × 0.1 | The interest gained in 1 term is p × r (p is the principal, r is the rate of interest in percentage)
The interest gained in 3 terms is 6000 × 0.1 × 3 | The interest gained in t terms is p × r × t
The total amount at the end of an FD of 3 years is 6000 + (6000 × 0.1 × 3). | The total amount at the end of an FD of t years is p + (p × r × t) = p + prt = p (1 + rt).
With Compounding
Here, the interest gained every term/year is added back to the FD. Therefore, the principal amount increases after every term, and as a result, the interest gained every term also increases proportionately.
The total amount in the FD after Year 1 is (6000) × 1.1 (principal for Year 1) | The total amount in the FD after Year 1 is (p) × (1 + r) (principal for Year 1)
The total amount in the FD after Year 2 is (6000 × 1.1) × 1.1 (principal for Year 2) | The total amount in the FD after Year 2 is p × (1 + r) × (1 + r) (principal for Year 2)
The total amount in the FD after Year 3 is (6000 × 1.1 × 1.1) × 1.1 (principal for Year 3) | The total amount in the FD after Year 3 is p × (1 + r) × (1 + r) × (1 + r) (principal for Year 3)
The total amount in the FD after t years is 6000 × (1.1 × 1.1 × 1.1….. × 1.1) [t times] = 6000 × (1.1)ᵗ. | The total amount in the FD after t years is p × (1 + r) × (1 + r) × ….. × (1 + r) [t times] = p × (1 + r)ᵗ.
Suppose we want to know the expression/formula to find the total interest amount gained at the end of the maturity period. What would be the formula for each of the two options? (Math Talk)

content.text:
Textbook text (verbatim):
Decline
Several items or materials lose financial value over time. Suppose someone buys a bike at your home for ₹1,00,000 and after a few years they want to sell it. The value of the bike at that time will be less than ₹1,00,000. It could depend on various factors, including how many years have passed since the purchase, how many kilometres the vehicle has been used for, if there has been any damage, or if any parts have been replaced. This is called depreciation - reduction of value due to use and age of the item.
Example 10: A TV is bought at a price of ₹21,000. After 1 year, the value of the TV depreciates by 5%. Find the value of the TV after one year.
(Method A) The amount of reduction in the value is 5% of 21,000 = 0.05 × 21,000 = 1050. The current value is 21,000 - 1050 = 19,950.
(Method B) The value of the TV after 1 year will be 95% of the current value = 95% of 21,000 = 0.95 × 21,000 = 19,950.
The value of the TV after 1 year will be ₹19,950.
Example 11: The population of a village was observed to be reducing by about 10% every decade. If the current population is 1250, what is the expected population after 3 decades?
(Method A) The population 1 decade later will be 0.9 times the population of the current decade. Therefore, the population after 1 decade will be 1250 × 0.9. The population after 2 decades will be 1250 × 0.9 × 0.9. The population after 3 decades will be 1250 × 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.9 = 911.25.
(Method B) First decade’s decrease = 0.1 × 1250 = 125. Population after 1 decade = 1250 - 125 = 1125. Second decade’s decrease = 0.1 × 1125 = 112.5 ≅ 112. Population after 2 decades = 1125 - 112 = 1013. Third decade’s population decrease = 0.1 × 1013 = 101.3 ≅ 101. Population after 3 decades = 1013 - 101 = 912.
Rounding off, we can say that the expected population after 3 decades will be around 910.

content.text:
Teaching plan:
1. Short why: decline is compounding in reverse. Each step keeps (1 − r) of the current value, so multiply by 0.95 or 0.9 repeatedly.
2. A decade-by-decade table shows the value shrinking, and each drop gets smaller because the base shrinks.
3. Point out why Method B gives 912 while Method A gives 911.25: rounding at each step.

topic_objective.objective_text: Students calculate interest with and without compounding, generalise the amounts to p(1 + rt) and p(1 + r)^t, and apply repeated multiplication to growth and decline. Compounding shows how a percentage of a growing base turns steady addition into exponential growth.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students define principal, rate of interest and per annum, and calculate the amount after one year as 110% of the principal, such as ₹6000 becoming ₹6600.
Students compare deposits with and without compounding year by year, and explain why compounded interest grows every year while simple interest stays the same.
Students derive p(1 + rt) and p(1 + r)^t from year-by-year amounts, write the rate as a decimal, and use the formulas to compare loans, deposits and populations.
Students calculate depreciation and population decline by multiplying by (1 minus the rate) at each step, and explain why rounding at every step changes the answer slightly.

media.title: Coupon Stacker
media.context: Class 8 'Fractions in Disguise', 1.3. The tool for one idea of the topic 'Percentages That Trick You': the second percentage is taken from a price that has already shrunk. Teaching Flow v3, Pattern A (AI drives every step): the AI controls everything; nothing on screen moves unless the AI moves it. It is used again on M4.S17.T17.C173. PLACEHOLDER: the tool is specified but not built yet; its url is reserved.
media.description:
A cake hangs at the top of the screen with a price tag reading Rs 200. Under it a blue price bar shows the full price with a scale from 0 to 100 and a bold label '100%, this is what the next coupon works on'. At the right waits a small stack of torn paper coupons, 30% OFF, 20% OFF and 50% OFF. The AI peels the coupons and nothing is clickable, so the student votes, predicts and answers aloud.

First the student restates the vote made earlier, Cakely with 30% plus 20% off, Cakify with 50% off, or the same, and predicts what Cakely's cake will cost. The AI sticks on the 30% coupon: that part of the bar dissolves in orange and the price falls to Rs 140. Then the key movement happens slowly. The 100% label and the whole scale slide down and re-attach to the shorter bar, renumbering themselves over its new length, while a faint ghost of the old, longer bar stays behind. The student is asked what the 20% coupon takes 20% of, and answers Rs 140, not Rs 200. The AI applies it, Rs 28 comes off, and the price is Rs 112. A second bar shows Cakify's single 50% coupon leaving Rs 100, so Cakify is cheaper.

Next the AI clears the cake and puts the coupons on the other way, 20% first and 30% second, and the price lands on Rs 112 again, so the order does not matter. A line under everything collects the multipliers, times 0.7 then times 0.8, giving times 0.56: you pay 56% and save 44%, not 50%. If an answer is off, the hints come in order. First: after the first discount what is the new price, and is the 20% taken from Rs 200 or from that? Then: write both steps as multipliers, times 0.7 and then times 0.8. A retry follows with 10% off and then another 10% off a Rs 500 bag, which should give Rs 405. The student learns that percentages applied one after another multiply and do not add, because each one is taken from the price that has already shrunk.

screen: Top: a cake with a price tag hanging from it. The tag shows the current price in large `ink` and updates as coupons are applied.

Right side: a small stack of paper coupons, each drawn with a dotted tear-edge and a printed percentage (30% OFF, 20% OFF, 50% OFF). The AI peels one off the stack and sticks it onto the tag; the peel-and-stick is a real animation, about 400 ms.

Centre, the price bar: a horizontal bar whose length is the current price, filled `fill`. Attached beneath it is a scale running 0 to 100, and a bold label reading "100%, this is what the next coupon works on."

The critical animation. When a coupon is applied: (1) the discounted portion of the bar dissolves in `bad-soft` and falls away; (2) the bar shortens; (3) the 100% label and the entire 0 to 100 scale detach, slide down, and re-attach to the new, shorter bar, re-numbering themselves across its shorter length. This slide takes a full 600 ms, slower than everything else in the chapter, because it is the lesson. Everything else in this tool exists to set up that one movement.
A ghost outline of the previous, longer bar stays faintly visible behind the new one, so the student can see how much the base shrank.
Comparison strip at the bottom: the single-50%-coupon result (₹100) can be drawn as a second bar below for direct comparison.
Multiplier readout: a line under everything shows the running multipliers as they accumulate: × 0.7 then × 0.7 × 0.8 = × 0.56, with the final "you pay 56%, so you saved 44%" appearing last.
Order swap: the AI can clear and re-apply the coupons in the opposite order to show the answer is unchanged.
Nothing is clickable.

AI asks: "So when I put the twenty percent coupon on, it takes twenty percent of which number?" (waits) "One forty. Not two hundred."

AI shows the multipliers: ×0.7 then ×0.8 = ×0.56. "Fifty-six percent of the price. Forty-four percent off."

Tricky Percentages
Would You Rather?
You have won a contest. The organisers offer you two options to choose from:
Option A: You deposit ₹100 and you get back ₹300.
Option B: You deposit ₹1000 and you get back ₹1500.
What is the percentage gain each option gives? You can choose any option only once. Which option would you choose? Why? (Math Talk)
While comparing percentages, we have to be mindful that we are comparing fractions or proportions and not absolute values.
A provision store is offering a stock clearance sale. Customers can choose one of the two options - 20% discount or ₹50 discount - for any purchase above ₹150. Which option would you choose if you want to:
(i) buy items worth ₹180 (ii) buy items worth ₹225 (iii) buy items worth ₹300

Teaching plan:
1. Let the student choose first and defend the choice; both choices can be sensible.
2. Short why: percentages compare rates; your wallet feels amounts. A (200% gain) is the better rate; B (₹500 gain) is more money. Which you prefer depends on your goal.
3. For the discount question, find the break-even: 20% of the bill equals ₹50 when the bill is ₹250. Below that, take ₹50; above it, take 20%.

content.text:
Textbook text (verbatim):
Example 12: A bakery called Cakely is offering a 30% + 20% discount on all cakes. Another bakery called Cakify is offering a 50% discount on all cakes. Would you rather choose Cakely or Cakify if you want the cheaper cost?
It seems that both the options should give the same benefit. Although mathematically 30% + 20% is the same as 50%, the usage of 30% + 20% in shopping means compounding.
Suppose you want to buy a cake worth ₹200.
Cakely’s 30% + 20% →
Applying the 30% discount → the price of cake is ₹200 - ₹60 = ₹140.
Applying the 20% discount on ₹140 → the price of cake is ₹140 - ₹28 = ₹112.
Cakify’s 50% →
The 50% discount makes the price of the cake ₹100.

content.text:
Teaching plan (logic first):
1. Key idea: successive percentages multiply, they don't add: 0.7 × 0.8 = 0.56, so you pay 56%. That is a 44% total discount, not 50%.
2. The same idea appears in compounding (5.2) and in the final Figure it Out Q4 and Q10: percent of a percent.
3. Close the story: Cakify is cheaper. Your vote at the start was a guess; now you have a proof. If the student voted Same at the start, celebrate the change of mind.

content.text:
Textbook text (verbatim):
A Mishap
Example 13: After Surbhi bought cookware from the wholesaler, she kept a profit margin of 50% on all the products. To clear off the remaining stock, she thought she would offer a 50% discount and come out without any loss.
(i) Do you think she didn’t make any loss?
(ii) If she had sold goods (originally) for ₹12,000 after discount, how much loss did she incur? What is the percentage loss?
(iii) What should have been the percentage discount offered so that she sold the goods at the price she had bought (i.e., no profit or loss)?
Let us model the situation first.
Suppose the worth of the products she bought from the wholesaler is x.
The worth corresponding to the selling price (with a 50% margin) is 1.5x.
A 50% discount on this price will make the worth 0.75x.
(Bars: x - Price bought at; 1.5x - Selling price including profit; 0.75x - After discount)
(i) This means the selling price is 3/4 of the price the goods were bought at, i.e., a 25% loss.
(ii) If she had sold goods worth ₹12,000,
0.75x = 12,000
x = 16,000.
She lost ₹4000.
(iii) To sell the goods at the same price, the discount offered should be
1.5x - d × (1.5x) = x
d = 1/3 = 0.33.
The discount offered should have been 33.33%.

content.text:
Teaching plan:
1. This is 6.2's idea applied to a real mistake. Ask for a prediction (loss or no loss?) and then use the bar model with two stacked bars: x, then 1.5x, then 0.75x.
2. Short why: the +50% is taken from x, but the -50% is taken from the bigger 1.5x, so the fall is larger than the rise.
3. (iii) With the bar: to go from 1.5x back to x, remove 0.5x out of 1.5x, which is 1/3, about 33.33%.
4. Ariba and Arun: Switch base. Arun's marbles as 100% gives Ariba 120%. Switching to Ariba's as 100% gives Arun 100/120, about 83.33%.

content.text:
Worked: After the 50% markup and the 50% discount, Surbhi's sales came to ₹12,000. How much did she pay for the goods, and what was her loss, in rupees and as a percentage?
1. The sale price is 1.5x × 0.5 = 0.75x
2. 0.75x = 12,000, so x = 16,000
3. Loss = 16,000 − 12,000 = 4000
4. 4000 out of 16,000 is 25%
Answer: Cost ₹16,000; loss ₹4000, which is 25%

maths_rules: the board has eight numbered lines, one per part of the chapter, each naming the 100% there
line 1, fraction to percentage: the 100% is the whole, rebuilt as 100
line 2, percent of a quantity: the 100% is the quantity itself

line 4, percentage change: the 100% is the original value, before the change
line 5, profit and loss: the 100% is what the shopkeeper paid
line 6, discount: the 100% is the marked price, the price on the tag

the wrong move: second 20% taken of Rs 200 gives Rs 40 off; it is struck through
line 8, compounding: the 100% each year is last year's amount, not the first year's

maths_rules: the board is 8 x 8; columns a to h are numbered 1 to 8 and rows 1 to 8; a square is black when column number + row number is even (a1 is black, as on a real board) and white when it is odd
a knight jumps two squares one way and one square across: 8 possible jumps from the middle of the board, fewer near an edge

hint 1 board: a knight on e4 (5 + 4 = 9, white) can jump to d2, f2, c3, g3, c5, g5, d6, f6, and all eight are black (sums 6, 8, 6, 10, 8, 12, 10, 12); a second knight on b1 (2 + 1 = 3, white) can jump to a3, c3, d2, all black
why the colour always changes: an L jump is 3 single steps along a row or column, each step changes the colour, and 3 changes leave the other colour
the wrong pair: knights on b1 and c3 look far apart, but c3 is 2 rows up and 1 column across from b1, one L jump; two knights side by side, such as a1 and b1, are safe because they are not an L apart

content.text:
Textbook text (verbatim):
SUMMARY
Percentages are widely used in our daily life.
Percentages are fractions with denominator 100. Percentages are denoted using the symbol ʻ%ʼ, pronounced ʻper centʼ. x% = x/100.
Fractions can be converted to percentages and vice versa. Decimals too can be converted to percentages and vice versa. For example, 4/10 = 0.4 = 40%. (Bar: 0% - 40% - 100%; 0 - 40/100 = 0.4 - 100/100 = 1)
We have learnt to find the exact number when a certain percentage of the total quantity is given.
When parts of a quantity are given to us as ratios, we have seen how to convert them to percentages.
The increase or decrease in a certain quantity can also be expressed as a percentage.
The profits or losses incurred in transactions, and tax rates, can be expressed in terms of percentages.
We have seen how a quantity or a number grows when compounded. Interest rates are a common example of compounding. If p is the principal, r is the rate of interest, and t is the number of terms, then the total amount after the maturity period is
Without compounding, p (1 + rt) - p remains the principal for all the terms.
With compounding, p × (1 + r) × (1 + r) × … × (1 + r) = p (1 + r)ᵗ - (labels: Principal for term 1, term 2, term 3, …, term t)
A situation or a problem can often be solved by describing it using a rough diagram. We have learnt to estimate and do mental computations to solve problems related to percentages.

content.text:
How to teach:
1. Optional, a fun break unrelated to percentages. Use a chessboard or any 8 × 8 grid.
2. Hint if stuck: a knight always jumps to a square of the other colour, so knights placed all on the same colour never attack each other. Eight is easy this way (up to 32 is possible).
3. One solution: all 8 knights on the white squares of the first two rows.

girls: 60% of each Grade 8 column of 10 = 6 squares; 4 columns x 6 = 24 squares out of 100

(ii) 24% of 160 = 0.24 x 160 = 38.4; the same by steps: 40% of 160 = 64 Grade 8 students, and 60% of 64 = 38.4
38.4 is not a whole number, so the book's numbers cannot all be exact; the honest answer is about 38
for a whole number of Grade 8 girls, 24/100 x total = 6/25 x total must be whole, so the total must be a multiple of 25: 150 gives 60 Grade 8 and 36 girls; 200 gives 80 and 48

video_script.anchor: Selling price of 3 pencils = cost of 5 pencils. Profit or loss? What percent?
video_script.design: One idea: when no prices are given, invent a cost, and measure the profit against what was paid. It assumes profit percent on cost price. The wrong idea: to divide the gain by the money received. The anchor stays all video; the pencil bars carry from the ground to the idea; one clear, before the recap. Adapted from the Teaching Flow's 'The Pencil Seller', keeping its ten rupee pencil; its closing check is redone with a three rupee pencil, and its 'sixty-seven percent markup' rounding is written as 66.67 percent.
video_script.wrong_move: A common slip is to measure the gain of two pencils' worth against five pencils, the money taken in, and say forty percent; the three pencils sold cost only thirty rupees, so the base he used is the wrong bar.
maths_rules: the book gives no prices: the selling price of 3 pencils equals the cost price of 5 pencils
invent a cost: one pencil costs Rs 10 (any cost works; 10 keeps the sums friendly)
cost of 5 pencils = 5 x 10 = Rs 50; this Rs 50 is what he receives for 3 pencils
selling price of one pencil = 50 / 3 = 16.666..., about Rs 16.67
profit on one pencil = 50/3 - 10 = 20/3 = 6.666..., about Rs 6.67
the same on 3 pencils: he paid 3 x 10 = Rs 30, received Rs 50, profit Rs 20; 20 / 30 = 2/3 = 66.67%
for any cost c: selling price of one pencil = 5c/3; profit = 2c/3; profit percent = 2/3 x 100 = 66.67%
recap check with a cost of Rs 3: 5 x 3 = Rs 15 for 3 pencils, so one sells for Rs 5; profit Rs 2 on Rs 3 = 2/3 = 66.67%
the wrong move: gain of 2 pencils' worth measured against 5 pencils' worth, 2/5 = 40%; the base should be the cost of the 3 pencils sold, Rs 30, not the Rs 50 received
bars on one scale: cost of 3 pencils = 30 units, money received = 50 units; the gain piece is 20 units
video_script.payoff_line: He makes a profit of about sixty-six point six seven percent.

final_answer.spoken: a profit of about sixty-six point six seven percent

video_script.substitution: Invent a cost for one pencil, then measure the profit against what he paid.

media.teaching_notes: The question has no rupees, so invent a cost; the answer does not depend on it. Watch for the base slip: two pencils' worth out of five gives forty percent, but profit is measured against what he paid for three, so it is two thirds, about 66.67 percent.

video_script.anchor: Fares up 3% last year, up 4% this year. Total rise over 2 years?
video_script.design: One idea: a rise on top of a rise is measured on the grown fare, so the growth factors multiply. It assumes the multiplier idea (up 3% is times 1.03). The wrong idea: to add the percents. The anchor and the ticket bars stay from the ground to the recap; one clear, before the recap. video_script.wrong_move: A common slip is to add three and four and say seven percent; the ticket drawn at each step shows the second rise is taken on Rs 103, not Rs 100, so the ticket ends a little above Rs 107.
maths_rules: a ticket that cost Rs 100 two years ago is used to see the rises (100 is chosen so rupees read as percent)
last year: up 3% of 100 = Rs 3, so the fare becomes 100 x 1.03 = Rs 103
this year: up 4% of 103 = 0.04 x 103 = Rs 4.12, so the fare becomes 103 x 1.04 = Rs 107.12
total rise = 1.0712 - 1 = 0.0712 = 7.12% of the fare two years ago
the extra beyond 3 + 4 = 7 is 0.12%: it is 4% of the 3% rise, 0.04 x 3 = 0.12 (on the Rs 100 ticket, 4% of Rs 3 = Rs 0.12)
the wrong move: 3% + 4% = 7%, which treats both rises as parts of the same Rs 100
the bars: Rs 100, then Rs 103, then Rs 107.12, drawn on one scale; the 4% piece on the second step is drawn on the Rs 103 bar
video_script.payoff_line: The fares went up seven point one two percent in all.

final_answer.spoken: seven point one two percent

video_script.substitution: Each year's rise is on last year's fare, so multiply the two growth factors.
video_script.wrong_answer: the fares went up seven percent

video_script.anchor: Length up 10%, area unchanged. The breadth goes down by what percent, exactly?
video_script.design: One idea: to keep a product the same, divide by what the other factor was multiplied by, and measure the fall against the old breadth. It assumes the multiplier idea and area as length times breadth. The wrong idea: to take ten percent off. The anchor stays all video; the rectangle stays from the ground to the recap; one clear, before the recap. Adapted from the Teaching Flow's 'Stretch the Rectangle', keeping its one over one point one reasoning and its 'two different hundreds' ending; real sizes of 20 m by 11 m are added so the numbers come out whole.
video_script.wrong_move: A common slip is to cut the breadth by ten percent; the rectangle, 22 m by 9.9 m, has area 217.8 square metres, less than the 220 it must keep, so a hatched strip of missing area shows it has shrunk.
maths_rules: area of a rectangle = length x breadth
the rectangle: length 20 m, breadth 11 m, area 20 x 11 = 220 square metres
length up 10%: 20 x 1.1 = 22 m
area must stay 220 square metres, so the new breadth = 220 / 22 = 10 m
breadth goes from 11 m to 10 m, a fall of 1 m out of 11 m, which is 1/11
in general: new length = 1.1 x length, so new breadth = breadth / 1.1 = 10/11 of the breadth = 0.9090... of it, about 90.91%; the fall is 1 - 10/11 = 1/11 whatever the rectangle
the wrong move: breadth down 10% gives 11 x 0.9 = 9.9 m; area 22 x 9.9 = 217.8 square metres, which is less than 220
the drawings keep one scale: 20 m, 22 m, 11 m, 10 m and 9.9 m in proportion
video_script.payoff_line: The breadth goes down by exactly one eleventh, about nine point zero nine percent.

final_answer.spoken: exactly one eleventh, nine and one eleventh percent, about nine point zero nine percent

video_script.substitution: The area must not change, so the breadth is divided by the same number the length is multiplied by.

video_script.anchor: Shop A: buy 1 get 1 free. Shop B: buy 2 get 1 free. Shop C: buy 3 get 1 free. Item Rs 100.
video_script.design: One idea: the discount is the free items out of everything you carry home. It assumes finding a percent from a fraction. The wrong idea: to compare free items with paid items. The anchor holds the three deals all video; the three rows of items stay from the ground to the recap; one clear, before the recap. The three parts share one video, solved in turn. Adapted from the Teaching Flow's 'Buy One Get One Free', keeping its order and its hundred rupee item; the letter A is spoken as eigh.
never_show: Shop B or Shop C as the best choice for 4 items
video_script.wrong_move: A common slip is to compare Shop B's one free item with the two he pays for and say fifty percent; the three items he carries home are worth three hundred rupees and he pays two hundred, so he saves one hundred out of three hundred, one third, not a half.
maths_rules: one item costs Rs 100 in every shop
Shop A, buy 1 get 1 free: pay 1 x 100 = Rs 100, carry home 2; each costs 100 / 2 = Rs 50
Shop B, buy 2 get 1 free: pay 2 x 100 = Rs 200, carry home 3; each costs 200 / 3 = 66.666..., about Rs 66.67
Shop C, buy 3 get 1 free: pay 3 x 100 = Rs 300, carry home 4; each costs 300 / 4 = Rs 75
cheapest to costliest: A (Rs 50), B (about Rs 66.67), C (Rs 75)
discount = free items / items carried home: A 1/2 = 50%; B 1/3 = 33.333..., about 33.33%; C 1/4 = 25%
exactly 4 items: A, buy 2 get 2, pay 2 x 100 = Rs 200; B, buy 2 get 1 (3 items, Rs 200) and buy 1 more at Rs 100, pay Rs 300; C, buy 3 get 1, pay Rs 300; choose A
the wrong move at Shop B: 1 free / 2 paid = 1/2 = 50%; the true base is the 3 items carried home, worth Rs 300; saved Rs 100 of Rs 300 = 1/3
the item rows are drawn one item = one equal box; paid items in one colour, free items in another
video_script.payoff_line: Shop eigh is the cheapest, then Shop B, then Shop C.

final_answer.value: (i) A Rs 50, B about Rs 66.67, C Rs 75 each; cheapest to costliest A, B, C. (ii) A 50%, B 33.33%, C 25%. (iii) Shop A, Rs 200 for 4 items
final_answer.spoken: fifty, about sixty-six rupees sixty-seven paise, and seventy-five rupees each, so eigh, then B, then C; discounts of fifty, thirty-three point three three and twenty-five percent; and for four items, Shop eigh at two hundred rupees

video_script.substitution: Count what you pay and what you carry home; the discount is the free items out of all the items you carry home.

media.teaching_notes: The hundred percent for the discount is everything you carry home, not what you pay for. Watch for 'one free for two paid is fifty percent' at Shop B; it is one free out of three received, about 33.33 percent.

interaction_points.answer: (i) A Rs 50, B about Rs 66.67, C Rs 75 each; cheapest to costliest A, B, C. (ii) A 50%, B 33.33%, C 25%. (iii) Shop A, Rs 200 for 4 items

media.description: A room of a hundred people is ninety-nine percent left-handed. The video follows the one right-handed person, who never leaves, and finds how small the room must become for him to be two percent of it.

video_script.anchor: 100 people, 99% left-handed. How many left-handers must leave to make it 98%?
video_script.design: One idea: when the whole changes, watch the part that stays fixed and ask what whole makes it the right percent. It assumes finding the whole from a part and its percent. The wrong idea: to think one person leaving moves the share by one percent. The anchor and the dot grid stay all video; one clear, before the recap. Adapted from the Teaching Flow's 'Ninety-Nine Percent Left-Handed'.
video_script.wrong_move: A common slip is to send one left-hander out; the room shows 98 left-handers out of 99 people, which is about 98.99 percent, still almost 99 percent, because the whole shrank too.
maths_rules: the room holds 100 people; 99% of 100 = 99 are left-handed; 1 is right-handed
only left-handers leave, so the 1 right-handed person always stays
now: 1 out of 100 = 1% right-handed
target: 98% left-handed means 100% - 98% = 2% right-handed
the right-handed person must be 2% of the room: 1 = 2% of the room, so the room = 1 / 0.02 = 50 people
people who leave = 100 - 50 = 50, all left-handed
check: 50 - 1 = 49 left-handers remain; 49 / 50 = 0.98 = 98%
the wrong move: 1 leaves, 98 left-handers out of 99 people; 98 / 99 = 0.98989..., about 98.99%, not 98%
the dot grid: 100 dots in a 10 by 10 grid, 99 in the left-handed colour and 1 in the right-handed colour; leaving dots fade out
video_script.payoff_line: Fifty left-handed people must leave the room.

final_answer.spoken: fifty left-handed people must leave

video_script.substitution: Watch the one right-handed person, who stays: when he is two percent, the whole room must be fifty.
video_script.wrong_answer: only one left-hander has to leave

media.teaching_notes: The trick is to watch the one person who stays: he must go from 1 percent to 2 percent of the room, so the room halves to 50. Watch for the guess 'one person leaves'; after one leaves, 98 out of 99 is still about 98.99 percent.

video_script.anchor: Ability to use a computer, by age and gender (2023): which statements are valid?
video_script.design: One idea: a percentage bar is a share of its own group, so check both bars, and never read it as a count. It assumes reading a bar graph and percent as a share. The wrong idea: to read taller bars as more people. The anchor and the graph stay all video; statements are ticked or struck one by one; one clear, before the recap. Adapted from the Teaching Flow's 'Reading the Graph Honestly', keeping its order and its closing trap; statement four is made exact, since the men's bar is exactly a quarter. The children's male bar is read from the book's graph as about five percent.
video_script.wrong_move: A common slip is to read the taller twenties bars as more people in their twenties; each bar is a percent of its own group, and two groups of different sizes are drawn as two small crowds with the same bar heights, so a share says nothing about how many people there are.
maths_rules: the book's bars, female then male, in percent: children 4 and about 5; teenage 24 and 29; twenties 26 and 37; thirties 14 and 25; forties 7 and 14; fifties 4 and 9; seniors (60 and above) 2 and 4
each bar is the percent of that age group and gender who can use a computer; bars are drawn to scale from these values
(i) valid: twenties are the tallest for women (26 > 24, the next highest) and for men (37 > 29, the next highest)
(ii) valid: female is below male in every group: 4 < 5, 24 < 29, 26 < 37, 14 < 25, 7 < 14, 4 < 9, 2 < 4
(iii) not valid: the bars are percents of each group, not head counts; they say nothing about how many people are in each group

(iv) not valid: a quarter is 25%; thirties are 14% (women) and 25% (men); 25% is exactly a quarter, not more, and 14% is less; the whole group lies between 14% and 25%, so it is not more than a quarter
(v) valid: 1 in 10 is 10%; seniors are 2% and 4%, both under 10%
(vi) not valid: half is 50%; twenties are 26% and 37%, both far below 50%
the wrong move: taller twenties bars read as more people; shown by two crowds of different sizes whose shares give the same bar height (such as 5 of 20 and 25 of 100, which are both 25%)
result: 3 statements valid, (i), (ii) and (v); 3 not valid, (iii), (iv) and (vi)
video_script.payoff_line: Statements one, two and five are valid, and the other three are not.

final_answer.spoken: statements one, two and five are valid, and three, four and six are not

video_script.substitution: Each bar is a share of its own group, so check both bars of the group, and never read a share as a head count.

content.text:
$1$. Compute each pair, then generalise with algebra.

objectives.objective_text: Students explain per cent as out of every hundred, using 25% as 25 of 100 squares, a quarter and 10 of 40 children, and state 50% of a quantity s as half of s.
Students convert fractions such as 3/4, 2/5 and 15/25 to percentages by scaling to 100, solving x/100 or reading a bar, and compare fractions with percentages without calculating.
Students write a percentage such as 24% or 40% as a fraction out of 100 and give at least two equivalent fractions for it.
Students compare 9/34 and 13/45 as percentages to explain why percentages exist, give reasons for choosing 100, and turn a percentage fact into a real-life sentence.
Students calculate the sugar Madhu and Madhav ate from 25% of 120 g and 35% of 95 g, and explain why a percentage alone cannot compare amounts taken from different wholes.
Students build 25%, 10%, 20%, 5%, 40% and 15% of numbers mentally from the blocks 50%, 10%, 5% and 1%, and describe recipes for 75%, 90%, 70% and 55%.
Students complete the fraction, decimal and percentage table, use 0.1 to find 10% of a quantity, and estimate a/b as a percentage to within 5 percentage points.
Students find a percentage of a whole in word problems, such as 80% of 75 marks, and convert a 2 : 7 ratio into a part-of-whole percentage after naming the whole.
Students find the whole from a given part by first finding one piece, such as 20% of the trip from 40% being 92 km, and then find the remaining 138 km.
Students interpret percentages above 100 as more than the whole, find 156%, 191% and 250% from sales and harvests, and write such percentages as fractions and decimals.
Students convert marks out of 50 and 80, and ingredients in 150 g and 400 g packs, into percentages to decide which score is better and which product has more of each ingredient.
Students calculate percentage increase and decrease as the change divided by the original amount, and explain why increased by 65% and 165% of describe the same change.
Students identify the cost price, marked price and selling price at each step of the sweater's journey, and calculate Kishanlal's ₹130 profit as selling price minus cost price.
Students calculate profit and loss percentages on the cost price, and find the cost price from a selling price and a profit percentage by finding one piece first.
Students find the selling price after a percentage loss or discount by multiplying by what is left, and find the cost price when a loss percentage and a selling price are given.
Students distinguish gross profit from net profit and explain why the same ₹250 profit is 50% of the cost but 33.33% of the revenue.
Students check a bill's CGST and SGST at 9% each and confirm that the total equals the subtotal plus 18% of the subtotal.
Students define principal, rate of interest and per annum, and calculate the amount after one year as 110% of the principal, such as ₹6000 becoming ₹6600.
Students compare deposits with and without compounding year by year, and explain why compounded interest grows every year while simple interest stays the same.
Students derive p(1 + rt) and p(1 + r)^t from year-by-year amounts, write the rate as a decimal, and use the formulas to compare loans, deposits and populations.
Students calculate depreciation and population decline by multiplying by (1 minus the rate) at each step, and explain why rounding at every step changes the answer slightly.
Students compare the percentage gain with the actual gain in two offers, and find the ₹250 break-even bill where 20% off saves exactly as much as ₹50 off.
Students apply successive discounts one after another, show that 30% then 20% off leaves 56% of the price, and prove which cake shop is cheaper.
Students explain why a 50% markup followed by a 50% discount causes a 25% loss, find the discount that breaks even, and restate 120% as about 83.33% from the other side.

Students solve the chapter's final mixed questions by naming the 100% first, choosing multipliers for successive change, working backwards from a changed amount and checking each answer against an estimate.
Students match each summary statement to an example from the chapter and state that the first step in every percentage problem is finding the 100%.

source_notes: In the profit and loss Figure it Out, the numbering restarts: 1 to 5, then 3 to 9. This plan calls them Q1 to Q12.
13/45 is 28.89% when rounded (the book prints 28.88%). 50/350 is 14.29% when rounded (the book prints 14.28%).
Final FIO Q2: the USA's share (about 4.2%) is not among the options, and 2% is printed twice.
Final FIO Q8(ii) gives 38.4 students, not a whole number, so the data cannot all be exact.
In the compounding formulas, the book says r is the rate of interest in percentage, but r must be used as a decimal (10% becomes 0.1).
The textbook has no answer key. Every answer in this plan was recomputed, and build.py recomputes them again.

Treating 'increased by 65%' and '165% of' as different things
Percent means out of 100 things, so 60% of 25 marbles is impossible
Believing x% of y is different from y% of x
With compounding, interest is the same every year

fear_free_rules: Estimate first, always, and never mark an estimate wrong. The textbook asks for this too: estimate first before solving.
Many methods are welcome. The AI presents them as a menu (Which one feels like yours?) rather than one correct way.
No scores during learning. Checks are at most 5 items, never timed, and never shown as marks.
Spot the slip shows a common slip, written without any named character; the slip is sensible. The student is the helper, never the one at fault.
A confident wrong answer is celebrated as a great-catch moment. Research on the hypercorrection effect shows these are the errors most likely to be fixed.
Easy first. Every question set opens with a question almost every student gets right.
Money and shopping contexts (discounts, sales, bills) are used because students already have intuitions there. The AI builds on those intuitions instead of replacing them.
The one-line rescue for the whole chapter: Draw the bar. Mark the 100%. Then ask what fraction of the bar you need.

spaced_revision.rule: Four questions per quiz, after about 2, 7 and 21 days. Low-stakes and not scored for marks. A question answered with 😎 certain twice is retired.
